tasks.sourceText: Hormones and Peptides for Skin

Designed toward future CME accreditation, this post-graduate clinical course prepares aesthetic and dermatologic clinicians to appraise the endocrine physiology of skin, differentiate pathognomonic endocrine cutaneous signs from isolated cosmetic presentations, evaluate the GRADE evidence and pharmacodynamics of cutaneous peptides and incretin therapies, and navigate regulatory and liability boundaries without promoting unapproved dosing protocols or commercial bias.

Continuing professional education for licensed clinicians and allied providers. Every learner gets the same evidence, regulatory status and safety content; what each may do with it — prescribe, recommend, administer, or refer — follows their own licence and scope, and the course adapts its practice guidance to that role. It informs clinical reasoning; it is not a protocol, contains no dosing, and does not replace specialist input, formal guidelines or individual judgment.
Educational content for clinicians. It does not prescribe, and it never restates an evidence grade above what the source assigns to the specific indication.

Regulatory statements name their jurisdiction and date. US status (FDA, 503A/503B compounding) is given in the lesson text; status in the United Kingdom, the European Union, Portugal, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates (federal, with Dubai and Abu Dhabi where they differ) is given in each moment's regulatory note, read from each regulator's own primary sources in September 2026, and the learner's own country is shown first. The US compounding categories have no equivalent in the other jurisdictions. Check the live status with the national regulator before acting.
Designed toward future CME accreditation. No CME or CE credit is currently offered.

Every row returned was 'Active'; the directory has no status filter, so withdrawn or cancelled registrations may not appear. Rows give classification, strength, form, manufacturer, status and registration date; detail pages add dispensing mode and a therapeutic category but no indications. Quotes join table cells with ' | ' and page fields with spaces; '…' marks omitted cells or fields. narrative review · academic · role: transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios · PMID 27104977 · Not cited by either guide; added to support the RNA-versus-protein step.

cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells after genotoxic stress (+ prostate tumours after chemotherapy) · academic · role: defines the SASP (IL-6, IL-8 and other secreted factors) — the concept the guide uses · PMID 19053174 · Not cited by either guide; the primary behind 'SASP'.

human skin tissue bank, cross-sectional (0–20, 21–70, 71–95 years) · academic · role: p16-positive cells are more numerous in older skin, in both epidermis and dermis · PMID 16911562 · Not cited by either guide.

cohort (Leiden Longevity Study), n=178, aged 45–81, sun-protected upper-inner-arm biopsies · academic; one co-author from Unilever; NIH and Cancer Research UK grants · role: senescent-cell counts in human skin track with elastic-fibre changes, facial wrinkles and perceived age, independent of chronological age; lowest vs highest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked ~3 years younger · PMID 26286607 · Not cited by either guide.
narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 5 — senescent cells accumulate in several human skin compartments; cell types respond differently · PMID 34166688 · Verified.

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 6 — no universal biomarker identifies senescent cells unequivocally; markers by skin compartment · PMID 30190724 · Full text (PMC6115505) read: it does not discuss estrogen loss or hormone responsiveness, which A&RE ch.7 cites it for.

narrative review (no new data) · three authors from L'Oréal and a senolytic-field investigator; declares no competing interests · role: how dermatologic senotherapy stands in 2026: a review of mechanism and prospects; transient senescence aids wound repair · PMID 42417965 · Not cited by either guide.

cross-sectional reference measurements of forearm skin · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 1 — skin collagen falls with age and is lower in women at all ages · PMID 1220811 · The abstract gives no annual rate; the guide's '~1% per year' could not be checked and is not taught.

human skin sections (18–29 vs 80+ years) and isolated dermal fibroblasts · academic · role: aged fibroblasts make less procollagen and are less attached to and stretched by collagen — two routes to lower synthesis · PMID 16723701 · Not cited by either guide.

aged (>80) vs young (21–30) human skin in vivo, plus organ and collagen-lattice culture · academic · role: more fibroblast MMP-1 in aged human dermis; fragmented collagen lowers fibroblast stretch and raises MMP-1 and oxidants — a self-perpetuating loop · PMID 19116368 · Not cited by either guide.

narrative review with new data · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 2 — UV drives the matrix breakdown of photoageing, and photoageing and chronological ageing share molecular pathways · PMID 12437452 · Verified.

mouse (INK-ATTAC transgene) · academic · role: A&RE ch.13 ref 2 — clearing p16-positive cells from one year of age extended median lifespan and delayed kidney, heart and fat deterioration; skin was checked for safety only (thickness, fibrosis), and clearance during healing slowed wound closure (Extended Data Fig. 10) · PMID 26840489 · Verified.

mouse, plus human adipose-tissue explants · several authors hold a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds senolytic patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 1 — senescent cells cause dysfunction when transplanted; senolytics improved function and post-treatment survival in old mice · PMID 29988130 · Verified.

regulator guidance note · regulator · role: UK specials: the regulation 167 exemption is narrowly drawn because specials may not have been assessed for safety, quality and efficacy (1.5); an unlicensed product should not be supplied where an equivalent licensed product can meet the patient's special needs, and 'special need' excludes cost, convenience or operational needs (2.2–2.3); a UK-licensed product, even off-label, should be used before an unlicensed one (2.4); manufacturers need a Manufacturer's 'Specials' Licence and GMP-inspected sites (4.1); particular specials must not be advertised (7.1); products prepared in a pharmacy under section 10 are also unlicensed medicines (1.6); Appendix 2 hierarchy: UK licensed, then off-label, then imported licensed product, then UK special (GMP-inspected but otherwise unassessed), with products that are not medicines in their country of origin, such as supplements, least acceptable · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200). Module 01 · The skin as an endocrine organ
The skin makes its own hormones.

This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

Module 01 · Opening film
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling.

Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.

Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Four units
Epidermis, dermis, subcutis and the adnexa each hold cells that make hormones and cells that react to them, from keratinocytes and fibroblasts to fat cells and mast cells.
Three routes
Signals pass between neighbouring cells, along sensory nerves, and into the blood, where they can reach distant organs.
What kind of evidence
The framework is drawn from cell, tissue and animal work. It explains how skin behaves; each finding in this module is labelled by the evidence behind it.

A steroid factory with local axes.

Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Local or systemic
Three directions of traffic.

Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.

Local loop
Body to skin

Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin
Local loop. Made and used where it is produced; the functional proof comes from mice that cannot make it in keratinocytes and develop skin inflammation.
UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to the liver
Skin to body. Vitamin D3 made in the skin is released into the circulation and activated elsewhere. Established human physiology.
Violaceous striae, thin skin and easy bruising in Cushing syndrome
Body to skin. Systemic cortisol excess acting on the dermis. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome as a reason to refer promptly.
Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol, then switch off their own CRH
Local loop, with its own feedback, running with no blood supply or nerves attached. Human tissue, ex vivo.
Skin converts circulating precursors into androgens and estrogens that add to the body's supply
Skin to body. Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids, more so in older people; the evidence is mainly biochemical.
Dry, coarse skin and myxoedema in hypothyroidism
Body to skin. Circulating thyroid hormone sets epidermal turnover and dermal matrix; the skin signs track the systemic deficit.
Scalp follicles convert testosterone to DHT, which shrinks susceptible follicles
Local loop. 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit makes DHT where it acts; the guide names it the substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia and hirsutism.
Seven placed. Three local loops, two signals the skin sends out, and two it receives.

What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.

The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment

Thinning and bruising, coarse dry skin, new acanthosis nigricans: each points to a systemic axis before it points to a serum.

The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly.
Where local biology fits
Local loops explain how skin behaves day to day. The guide calls them foundation, never a reason to dose anyone with a hormone.

The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.
When a skin pattern suggests a systemic disorder, assess or refer before any cosmetic plan, and record that you considered it. Local skin biology is no basis for prescribing a hormone for appearance.
If you see new striae, rapid bruising, sudden hair change or signs of virilisation, record them and raise them with the prescriber before the next treatment.

Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.

The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
What it measured
RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes, cell by cell, across 47 human tissues including skin.
What it predicted
Which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond, including unexpected sites outside the classic glands.
What it leaves open
Whether a cell actually makes and releases the hormone, and whether that hormone does anything there.

Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.
A grid of small tissue tiles with a skin tile at the centre, where some cells carry receptor cups and a few hold outlined granules, marking cells predicted to respond to or make a hormone.
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.

The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.

Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D
Claims built on receptors
Receptors explain how a topical could act. Whether it does is a question for a human trial.
Local enzymes
Steroid-metabolising enzymes in skin change potency, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts.
Sunscreen and vitamin D
Artificial-UV experiments show sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis; field trials of daily use did not lower blood levels. High-protection products have not been trialled.

Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.

When a product or protocol is justified by 'skin has receptors for it', ask for the human trial before you prescribe. Assess vitamin D on clinical grounds, and do not advise patients to drop sun protection.
If a patient says they stopped sunscreen to raise their vitamin D, note it and pass it to the prescriber; the trials do not support stopping.
Describe receptor-based product claims as hypotheses unless a human trial backs them, keep sun-protection advice unchanged, and send vitamin D questions to a prescriber.

Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.

A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
A safety mechanism
A damaged cell stops dividing for good, which guards against cancer and helps wound repair.
The secretory phase
It stays active and releases inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors, first catalogued in cultured human cells.
What we see in human skin
Older skin holds more cells carrying the marker p16 in epidermis and dermis. No single marker is definitive.

Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.

Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.

In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.

Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.

A collagen-fragmentation loop

Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.

Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet

A publicly funded Australian trial of 903 adults: daily sunscreen meant about a quarter less skin ageing over four and a half years.
Retinoids

Senotherapies
Biomarker pilots only, so far. They sit below the levers that already have outcome data.

Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.

Module 02 · Opening film
Systemic hormones and the skin

Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist. Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the receptors to respond to them. They also carry an enzyme called eleven beta HSD one, which turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples that enzyme works harder with age and in sun-exposed skin, and it sets local cortisol independently of the level in the blood. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice bred without the enzyme kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Hold all of this in the mechanism register. It comes from biopsies, cultured cells and mice, and it says nothing yet about how a patient's face will age.
Mechanism
The skin regenerates its own cortisol.

Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.

11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells

Why it matters for ageing
Cortisol slows collagen synthesis in fibroblasts, and knockout mice kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Whether this drives visible ageing in people has not been tested.

The evidence
Rare, and usually from a prescription.

Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)

A round, puffy face in an aesthetic clinic is almost always something other than Cushing's syndrome, and when cortisol excess is real it most often comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is already using.

It does not mean you can dismiss it. The guideline recommends testing when discriminating features are multiple and progressive or unusual for age, and some groups, such as people with poorly controlled diabetes, carry a higher rate.
What changes in practice
Reassure the many, refer the few.

When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.

Lesson 2.2 · Concept
Estrogen and the dermis.

Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.

Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors in sun-protected and sun-damaged sites alike. In a vehicle-controlled study, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in the hip skin of postmenopausal women; in photoaged forearm and facial skin, the same treatment made no measurable difference. Small biopsy studies from the nineteen eighties and nineties found that skin collagen and thickness fall after menopause, and that the fall follows years since the last period more closely than birthdays. Keep two questions apart as you go. One is what estrogen does in the dermis. The other is whether giving it changes how a face ages, and those answers come from different trials.
Two panels of dermis: in sun-protected skin, receptor-bearing cells lay down new collagen; in sun-damaged skin, the same cells sit among fragmented, clumped fibres with no new collagen.

The evidence
One to two per cent a year.

In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.

Regulatory status and indications
Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.

In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning; skin did not become an indication. The North American Menopause Society's 2022 statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone protection when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and finds insufficient evidence for compounded 'bioidentical' hormones. Under US rules an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug. For the skin itself, daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it, and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine facial wrinkles.

For the skin itself: daily sunscreen and a retinoid

Where does that leave hormone therapy for skin? In the United States, as of February 2026, the approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products the prevention of bone loss. In late 2025 the FDA asked manufacturers to remove heart, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, and it approved the first revised labels in February 2026. Skin still appears nowhere among the uses. The menopause society's 2022 position statement finds the balance favourable for symptoms and bone when therapy starts before sixty or within ten years of menopause, and it finds too little evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms is the one use aimed at the tissue itself. For the face, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid carry better evidence than any hormone. Treat symptoms on their merits, and count any skin change as a bonus.

Prescribe hormone therapy for its labeled indications and the position statement's timing, and record that skin was discussed only as a secondary effect. Do not prescribe systemic or topical estrogen for wrinkles alone, and prefer licensed products (FDA-approved in the US) to compounded 'bioidentical' preparations.

If a patient asks for 'hormones for my skin', ask about hot flashes, sleep and vaginal symptoms, record what she says, and route those symptoms to the prescriber. The skin concern stays with skin-directed care.

In the US, a cream sold as containing estrogen for the face is regulated as a drug, and compounded 'bioidentical' products lack efficacy and safety data. Menopausal symptoms are a conversation for a prescriber; sun protection is advice you can give.

In the UK, as of September 2026, HRT products such as estradiol patches and gel are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis in women at high risk of fracture; skin is not among their uses. A compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine in the UK, and MHRA guidance puts a licensed product first when one can meet the need. On the UK medicines compendium, topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments.

In the EU, the harmonised core product information for HRT (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as its indications; skin is not an indication. EU cosmetics law prohibits oestrogens, progestogens and tretinoin in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II), and anti-wrinkle products containing tretinoin marketed as cosmetics are illegal cosmetics.

In Portugal, as of September 2026, the estradiol HRT products Estreva gel and Estrofem tablets are authorised for symptoms of oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women. The topical tretinoin product Ketrel cream is authorised and prescription-only on INFARMED's database, with indications for acne (except acne rosacea) and keratinisation disorders.

In Brazil, as of September 2026, estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy is registered and the Oestrogel label covers menopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, not skin ageing, while the Vitacid label for topical tretinoin names cutaneous photoageing as well as acne vulgaris. The Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) bars physicians from using hormones, in any formulation, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit (Resolution 1.999/2012), and from prescribing hormones marketed as 'bioidentical' or 'nano' without proof of superiority (Resolution 2.333/2023).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, registers estradiol products as Prescription Only Medicines, for example Oestrogel gel (since 11 November 2021). The EDE register lists therapeutic categories rather than indications, so it does not show whether any UAE label includes a skin indication (25 September 2026). Under the medicines law, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, a compounding pharmacy may not compound products that are essentially copies of EDE-approved products unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient.

Lesson 2.3 · Concept
Some syndromes show on the skin first.

A handful of inherited endocrine syndromes appear on the skin before the glands declare themselves. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common. In Carney complex, lentigines on the lips, eyelids and canthi, blue naevi and small skin myxomas sit alongside myxomas of the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN2A, an itchy, rippled, pigmented plaque between the shoulder blades can precede medullary thyroid cancer.

MEN1
Loss of the tumour suppressor menin. Multiple facial angiofibromas, identical to those of tuberous sclerosis, and truncal collagenomas.
Carney complex
Inactivating variants in PRKAR1A, the regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. Lentigines, blue naevi and myxomas of skin and heart, with Cushing's syndrome from the adrenal.
MEN2A
Activating RET variants, most often at codon 634 when the skin is involved. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis over the upper back, often found before the thyroid cancer.

Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofibromas, the same lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis, along with collagenomas on the trunk. In Carney complex, usually caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene, freckle-like lentigines cluster on the lips, eyelids and the corners of the eyes, alongside blue naevi and small skin myxomas. The same patients can develop myxomas in the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN two A, an itchy, rippled, darkened patch between the shoulder blades, called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, can appear long before medullary thyroid cancer. Each of these is a referral finding, and none of them is yours to diagnose alone.

The evidence
Eighty-eight per cent.

In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.

It does not mean a single facial papule is MEN1. This is one small referral-centre series, and angiofibromas have other causes, tuberous sclerosis above all.

Most endocrine skin signs you meet come from common disease. New generalised darkening, strongest in skin creases, scars, mucosa and sun-exposed skin, can signal primary adrenal insufficiency, which can turn into a life-threatening crisis. Hirsutism that appears fast, keeps progressing, or comes with a deepening voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely. Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance, pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease, and cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

Module 03 · Opening film
Fat, incretins and the ageing face

Facial shape depends on fat as much as on collagen. In three lessons you will separate what is known about the skin's own fat, sugar damage to the dermis, weight-loss drugs and the gut from what is still mechanism, marketing or an open question. Most people picture skin fat as one layer under the dermis. There is a second, thinner layer inside the reticular dermis itself, called dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and its new fat cells release cathelicidin, an antimicrobial peptide. Older mice lose much of that capacity, through TGF-beta signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in small cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain preadipocytes around the follicle that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not yet been measured. So hold two things apart when you hear about skin fat. The defence story is strong in mice and emerging in people. The ageing story in people is still a proposal.
Mechanism
The skin keeps its own fat.

Beneath the dermis lies subcutaneous fat. Within the reticular dermis itself sits a thinner layer, dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, its new fat cells release the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin, and the capacity fades with age through TGF-β signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not been measured.
A second fat layer inside the dermis
In mice: antimicrobial, and lost with age
In people: a different shape, and an open question about ageing
A second fat layer
Dermal white adipose tissue sits inside the reticular dermis, separate from the subcutaneous fat below. Fat as a whole is an endocrine organ that releases hormones such as leptin and adiponectin.
What it does in mice
The layer expands after skin infection and its fat cells release cathelicidin. Older mice lose much of this capacity, through TGF-β signalling.
What is known in people
Human dermal fat clusters in cones around hair follicles, and acne lesions contain preadipocytes that make cathelicidin. Its part in skin ageing is unmeasured.

Human evidence

Cadaver dissection shows that the face's subcutaneous fat sits in separate compartments, and facial ageing is partly how each compartment changes. Weight shows the same thing from the outside. In a study of 186 pairs of identical twins, the twin with the higher body-mass index looked older before about age 40 and younger after it.

It is an observational comparison of photographs. It does not show that gaining weight rejuvenates, or that fat loss on a drug changes the skin itself.
Mechanism
Sugar that sticks to collagen.

Glycation is a slow, non-enzymatic reaction. Reducing sugars attach to protein amino groups, rearrange into Amadori products and end as advanced glycation end products, or AGEs. On long-lived dermal collagen, AGEs form cross-links that stiffen the matrix. Through their receptor, RAGE, AGEs switch on inflammatory signalling in laboratory studies. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects B; the course grades the causal link to visible ageing D, because the human data are associations.

Cross-links stiffen long-lived collagen
RAGE signalling: shown in the laboratory
The reaction
Reducing sugars bind protein amino groups, form a reversible Schiff base, then a more stable Amadori product, and finally irreversible AGEs.
Two kinds of damage
Structural: AGEs cross-link collagen and elastin and stiffen the dermis. Signalling: AGEs bind RAGE, which drives NF-κB and inflammatory cytokines in cell and animal studies.
Where the grades differ
The Hormonaly endocrinology guide rates both B. The course grades the causal link to visible ageing D, because the human data are associations.

Glycation is chemistry before it is biology. Reducing sugars attach to the amino groups of proteins, rearrange into more stable products, and end as advanced glycation end products, known as AGEs. Dermal collagen lasts for years, so it collects AGEs, and they form cross-links that make the matrix stiffer. AGEs also bind a receptor called RAGE, which in laboratory studies switches on inflammatory signalling and enzymes that break down matrix. Keep the registers apart here. The chemistry, and the build-up of AGEs in human skin, are well documented. The idea that AGEs cause the wrinkles and laxity you see in clinic rests on laboratory and animal work plus human associations. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects grade B. This course grades the causal link D, and the next moment shows why.

The first product, the Schiff base, is reversible.
More stable Amadori product
It rearranges into a more stable Amadori product.
Irreversible AGEs
The reaction ends as advanced glycation end products, or AGEs, which are irreversible.
Cross-links stiffen long-lived collagen
Dermal collagen lasts for years, so it collects AGEs, and they form cross-links that make the matrix stiffer.
The chemistry is well documented; that AGEs cause visible ageing is graded D, because the human data are associations.
Human evidence
Fifteen years on the same collagen.

Human skin collagen turns over slowly; tissue analysis puts its half-life at about 15 years. In skin biopsies, glycoxidation products in collagen rose about five-fold between ages 20 and 85, and were up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes. Skin autofluorescence, a non-invasive reading, correlates moderately with those biopsy measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin.
estimated half-life of human skin collagen
Verzijl et al., 2000 · AGE content of skin collagen rises about five-fold from age 20 to 85 (Dyer et al., 1993)
Glycation damage accumulates on the same collagen for years, and faster with higher glucose exposure. That much is measured in human skin: direct, observational, GRADE C.
It does not show how much of visible ageing AGEs cause, or that any product reverses established cross-links. Skin autofluorescence is a surrogate reading of AGE load.

Lesson 3.2 · Concept
Two gut hormones, re-engineered.

GLP-1 and GIP are incretins, hormones the gut releases after a meal that amplify glucose-dependent insulin release; GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 is broken down within minutes. Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist, and tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In the US, as of September 2026, both are FDA-approved drugs for defined indications, set out in the next moment.
Incretins amplify insulin after meals
Semaglutide: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Tirzepatide: GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist
Incretins
GLP-1 from intestinal L-cells and GIP from K-cells amplify insulin release when glucose is high. GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite.
Engineered to last
Native GLP-1 is cleared within minutes by the enzyme DPP-4. The drug molecules are modified to last far longer in the blood.
Two molecules, four brands
In the US, semaglutide is sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, tirzepatide as Mounjaro and Zepbound, and the brand tells you the approved use.

After a meal, the gut releases two hormones called incretins, GLP-1 and GIP. Both amplify insulin release when glucose is high, and GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood before an enzyme breaks it down, so the drug molecules are engineered to last far longer. Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide activates both the GIP and the GLP-1 receptors. Those are the mechanisms. The regulatory facts sit in a separate register. In the United States, as of September 2026, both molecules are FDA-approved drugs, sold under one brand name for type 2 diabetes and another for chronic weight management, with further indications for the heart, the liver and sleep apnoea. The face appears nowhere on those labels, and that is where this lesson begins.
In the UK both are licensed by the MHRA, and tirzepatide's diabetes and weight-management uses share one brand, Mounjaro.

In the EU, semaglutide is a centrally authorised prescription medicine, as Ozempic and Rybelsus for diabetes and Wegovy for weight management (EMA and HMA, June 2024), and tirzepatide is authorised as Mounjaro (EU-wide, 15 September 2022) for diabetes and adult weight management, prescription-only. A search of the Union Register and EMA's medicines data on 25 September 2026 found no EU product named Zepbound.

Since 23 June 2025, GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines may only be sold with retention of the prescription (RDC 973/2025 and IN 360/2025).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and its register lists semaglutide as Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy and tirzepatide as Mounjaro; every entry checked is a Prescription Only Medicine. A search of the EDE register on 25 September 2026 found no product named Zepbound.

Human evidence
Large trials, measured on the scale.

In STEP-1, 1,961 adults without diabetes lost a mean 14.9% of body weight on semaglutide over 68 weeks, against 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1, 2,539 adults lost 15.0% to 20.9% on tirzepatide over 72 weeks, depending on dose, against 3.1% on placebo. Both Hormonaly guides grade weight management A. Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue.
mean weight loss in STEP-1 (semaglutide, 68 weeks) and SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide, highest dose, 72 weeks)
Placebo 2.4% and 3.1% · both trials industry-funded, both the basis for approval

These drugs produce large, reproducible weight loss in randomized trials: GRADE A for the approved indications. Part of what is lost is lean tissue, which is why the Hormonaly guide pairs treatment with protein and resistance training.
Neither pivotal trial measured facial fat, skin laxity or appearance. An A for weight loss says nothing about the face.
Four registers
'Ozempic face', answer by answer.
The phrase bundles four kinds of statement. Kept apart, they tell a patient far more than the headline does.
Mechanism
Volume loss
Losing fat deflates the superficial facial compartments and unmasks laxity that was already there.
Human evidence
Observational and small: C to D

One imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial, about 7% per 10 kg lost. A survey of 1,226 patients found sagging, facial volume loss and hair shedding reported more often the more weight was lost. A systematic review of the plastic-surgery literature found it limited by study bias. No randomized trial has measured the face.
Regulatory status (US, September 2026)
Hair loss labelled; facial change unlisted

Both labels list hair loss (about 3–6% on drug against about 1% on placebo, mostly in women, linked to weight reduction). The semaglutide label also lists altered skin sensation. Facial volume loss is not a labelled adverse reaction.
Open question
A direct drug effect?
Whether these drugs act on facial fat or skin cells beyond the effect of weight loss rests on cell studies and has not been tested in people.
So far, the evidence ties facial change to how much weight is lost.
UK product information also lists hair loss: 2.5% on Wegovy and 4.9% on Mounjaro in the weight-management trials, against 1.0% on placebo.

Lesson 3.3 · Concept
Inflammation that comes with age.

Inflammaging is the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age. In older adults, higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty and death. One proposed source is the gut. Inflammaging
A slow rise in background inflammation with age. Higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty, disability and death in older adults.
The gut hypothesis
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide crossing a leaky barrier is one proposed source, shown in mice and as a short rise after a fatty meal in a small human study.
Where the evidence stops
Measuring gut permeability is hard, and restoring the barrier has not been shown to improve disease outside the gut.

Ageing brings a slow rise in background inflammation, called inflammaging. It is low-grade and sterile, and in older adults higher IL-6 and C-reactive protein predict frailty, disability and death. One proposed source is the gut. In mice, a high-fat diet raises bacterial lipopolysaccharide in the blood, and infusing that endotoxin reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance. In twelve healthy men, a single high-fat meal raised plasma endotoxin within four hours. That is the mechanism usually called metabolic endotoxaemia, or leaky gut. The human evidence stops short of the skin. Measuring gut permeability is difficult, and a leading review concludes that it is still unproven whether restoring the barrier improves disease outside the gut. Hold that line as you look at what patients are sold.
Two views of the gut lining: one with closed junctions keeping small bacterial fragments out, the other with loosened junctions letting them pass into a blood vessel.
The evidence
Thirty-nine trials of probiotics for eczema.

An independent Cochrane review pooled 39 randomized trials, with 2,599 participants, of oral probiotics for eczema. Probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated symptoms, and investigator-rated severity fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference. A 2024 European task-force meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported a significant fall in severity scores.

The most direct test of 'treat the gut, help the skin' in a common inflammatory skin disease shows, at most, a small effect. GRADE B for little or no benefit a patient would notice.
It does not rule out benefit from particular strains or in particular groups, and it says nothing about skin ageing. Newer pooled analyses in children report small improvements.

What changes in practice

Patients often link their skin to their gut. Start where the evidence is. Diet quality, treatment of metabolic disease and the established treatment for the skin condition itself all come first. Be careful with tests. A widely used commercial zonulin assay was shown to detect proteins other than zonulin, so a result cannot tell you whether a gut is leaky. Be careful with products too. Probiotics are strain-specific, and their effects on eczema are small at best. The Hormonaly guide gives the popular gut-repair stack of glutamine, zinc carnosine and BPC-157 a grade of D. As of September 2026, in the United States, BPC-157 remains off the 503A bulks list after the July advisory-committee review. Investigational peptides come last, if at all. Whatever your role, name the evidence type before you name the product.

Treat the skin disease on its own evidence and metabolic disease directly. A zonulin result should not guide care. In the US, BPC-157 has no 503A bulks-list standing as of September 2026, so compounding it for gut repair is not an option.
If a patient brings a gut-repair kit or a zonulin result, record the products and the result and bring them to the prescriber. Do not interpret the test or advise on the products.

You can say that fibre-rich diets have strong evidence for metabolic health, that probiotics are strain-specific with small skin effects at best, and that injected or research peptides need a prescriber.
In the United Kingdom, an unlicensed peptide reaches a patient only through narrow routes, such as a special ordered for one patient's clinical need, which module seven sets out.

In the EU, Directive 2001/83/EC allows a medicine on the market only with a national or EU-wide marketing authorisation (Article 6(1)), while medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formulas) fall outside the directive and need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3). Each member state may also, under its own law, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, no medicine containing BPC-157 is listed in INFARMED's Infomed register (25 September 2026). A medicine is defined as any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease or that may be used or administered to restore, correct, or modify physiological functions through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento, Article 3). INFARMED does not authorise importing medicines for personal use, and a compounded medicine may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese Pharmacopoeia, the European Pharmacopoeia, pharmacopoeias of other States Parties to the European Pharmacopoeia Convention, or compendial scientific documentation (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Article 6).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that any substance must have undergone efficacy and safety assessments before it can be compounded, and that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or food supplement) and are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use. ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used exclusively in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, in force since 2 January 2025, bars importing, selling or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), and lets a physician prescribe a medicine never submitted for approval only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any research-use peptide on humans, or for treatment, outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH lets physicians prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status, and compounded peptides may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight (31 July 2026).

Where does the page overreach?
A patient shows you this fictional sales page for a 'gut–skin reset' kit. Which sentences does the evidence not support?
Background inflammation rises slowly with age; researchers call it inflammaging.
Supported. Inflammaging is the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age.
In older adults, higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty and death.
Supported, as a prediction: in older adults, higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty, disability and death.
Studies show that a high-fat diet raises gut bacterial toxin in the blood, and that the toxin causes weight gain and insulin resistance.
Shown in mice. There, a high-fat diet raised bacterial lipopolysaccharide in the blood, and infusing it reproduced weight gain and insulin resistance; the page leaves out the species.

Supported: in 12 healthy men, a single high-fat meal raised plasma endotoxin within four hours. A short rise in a small study; the human evidence stops short of the skin.

Not shown. Whether a leaky gut drives skin disease in people has not been shown.

Unproven. Restoring barrier function has not been shown to improve disease outside the gut.
A fibre-rich diet has strong evidence for heart and metabolic health.
Supported, for the heart and metabolism: the guide grades it A, and the review behind it rates certainty moderate. No trial has measured skin.

Module 04 · Opening film
Matrix peptides and wound healing

Most skin peptides reach your clinic before any evidence does. In three lessons you will sort them by what the human trials actually show, who paid for those trials, and where each one stands with the regulator. Start with the molecule. GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide that circulates in human plasma; it was first described in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex, GHK-Cu, is what skin-care labels mean when they say copper peptide. The proposed mechanism is that GHK-Cu delivers copper to enzymes that build and protect the dermal matrix, such as lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase, and shifts gene expression toward wound healing. Two things to hold on to. First, this is a mechanism, which explains why the peptide might work and leaves open whether it does. Second, most of this literature was written by the group that discovered the peptide. Keep both in mind when you reach the trials.

Mechanism
A plasma tripeptide with a copper habit.

GHK is a tripeptide found in human plasma, first described in 1973. Bound to copper it becomes GHK-Cu, which is proposed to deliver copper to enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and to switch on wound-healing and antioxidant gene programmes. Most of that mechanistic literature comes from the group that discovered the peptide.
Endogenous: GHK circulates in human plasma
Proposed: copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes
Mechanism register only — written largely by the originator
Where it comes from
GHK — glycyl-histidyl-lysine — was isolated from human plasma in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex is what the skin-care literature calls GHK-Cu.
What it is proposed to do
The proposed mechanism is copper delivery to enzymes that build and protect the matrix, plus broad changes in gene expression linked to wound healing.
Who wrote it
Much of this work, including the gene-expression reviews, comes from the peptide's discoverer. That does not make it wrong. It does make it a mechanism, and it is worth saying who proposed it.

Human evidence
One indexed randomized trial.

A search of PubMed in September 2026 found one randomized controlled trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin: 2006, healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing. The cosmetic trials cited for anti-ageing claims are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed. Both Hormonaly guides grade topical use C.
indexed randomized trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin
Miller et al., 2006 — healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing, not photoageing
The human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small: one small indexed trial plus sponsor-run cosmetic studies. GRADE C is the honest ceiling.
It does not show that GHK-Cu fails, that it treats photoageing, or anything about injecting it. A thin evidence base is an unknown, not a negative.

Keep the four answers apart.
Every peptide question has four separate answers. For GHK-Cu they point in different directions, which is exactly why they must not be blended into one sentence.

What changes in practice
Serum yes, syringe no.

Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation at GRADE C. Injected GHK-Cu is a different product: no randomized trials, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the US the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing.
Topical: modest, small-trial support
Injectable: anecdote, common local reactions
Say which route you mean every time

Here is what that means in the room. Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation, as long as you describe the evidence honestly: small trials, modest effects, grade C. Injected GHK-Cu is not the same product in a stronger form. There are no randomized trials of injection, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the United States the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing that covers non-injectable use. Whatever your role, name the route every time you talk about this peptide.

In the US, before prescribing a compounded topical, confirm the substance's current 503A status and that the pharmacy is working within it. Do not prescribe GHK-Cu for injection. Record that you discussed a product with small-trial evidence and the patient's reasons for choosing it.
If a patient tells you they inject GHK-Cu, record the product, where it was bought and any site reactions, and bring it to the prescriber. Do not advise on amounts or technique.
Describe topical GHK-Cu products as cosmetics with modest, small-trial support. Anyone injecting a copper peptide should be pointed to a prescriber, not to a better supplier.

In the UK, anything injected falls outside cosmetics law, and MHRA decides whether it is a medicine from its claims, form and use. In the UK, a GHK-Cu serum presented for appearance is a cosmetic, so there is nothing to prescribe.

In the EU, a substance or mixture intended to be injected is not considered a cosmetic product (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)); the EU borderline manual adds that a product in a vial or ampoule for use by injection cannot be considered a cosmetic product, and should not be marketed with a device that could allow injection or delivery below the epidermis. Whether a product qualifies as a cosmetic is decided case by case by national competent authorities, and the manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as one (version 5.5, June 2025).

In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by injection are not considered cosmetics (as of 25 September 2026), and medicines intended for parenteral administration are subject to medical prescription by law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 114(1)(d)).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist; an injectable product offered as a cosmetic is irregular. Products with 'GHK' in the product name appear as notified cosmetics in ANVISA's public cosmetics data (221 entries, 25 September 2026), and ANVISA cancelled several GHK-Cu cosmetic processes on 29 April 2026 without published reasons (RE 1.771/2026).

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) defines cosmetics as products with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and whether a product requires an Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) marketing authorisation, and in which category, is determined by an EDE classification letter based on its presentation, composition, use and design. In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed health facility (DHA, 29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (DoH, 31 July 2026).

Lesson 4.2 · Concept
Three families, one question: who ran the trial?

Signal peptides such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS, Matrixyl) are meant to tell fibroblasts to make matrix. SNAP-25 mimics (Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8) and Leuphasyl, an enkephalin analogue, are meant to quieten expression lines. Oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. All three families have a trial record, and in all three the question that matters most is who funded it.
Signal peptides: 'make more matrix'
SNAP-25 mimics: 'relax the line'
Oral collagen: the supplement aisle
Signal peptides
Palmitoylated fragments of matrix proteins, designed to mimic the signals that tell fibroblasts to repair. The palmitoyl tail helps them into the skin.
SNAP-25 mimics
Argireline copies the end of SNAP-25, a protein botulinum toxin cleaves. SNAP-8 is the maker's eight-residue extension. The premise is a gentler topical version of the same effect.
Oral collagen
Hydrolysed collagen taken by mouth, sold as a supplement, with more randomized trials than any topical peptide — and the clearest funding problem.

Lesson two covers three families that fill the cosmetic and supplement shelves. Signal peptides, like palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl, are fragments of matrix proteins meant to tell fibroblasts to make more collagen. SNAP-25 mimics, Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8, copy part of a nerve-terminal protein that botulinum toxin targets; the idea is a gentle, topical version of that effect. And oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. Every one of these has trials behind it. As you go through them, keep asking one question before any other: who ran the trial, and who paid for it.

What changes in practice
Cosmetic, supplement, drug: three rulebooks.

In the US, cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework. Oral collagen is a dietary supplement: it may not claim to treat disease, and product quality and content vary. Neither route has to prove efficacy before sale — which is why the funding question matters.
Cosmetic ingredient: no efficacy approval needed
Dietary supplement: no disease claims; quality varies
Say 'modest, small-trial' — never 'topical Botox'

Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub varies from brand to brand. That is the whole reason the funding question matters here. When no regulator asks for efficacy, the only efficacy data are the trials someone chose to pay for.
Nothing here needs a prescription. If you recommend a product, recommend it on evidence, name the grade, and disclose any relationship with the brand. The 'topical Botox' claim is not one to repeat.
When a patient asks which serum 'really works', the accurate answer is modest effects from mostly sponsor-funded trials. Do not describe any of them as an alternative to botulinum toxin.

The claim you can stand behind is modest, small-trial evidence. Supplements cannot be sold as treating a disease; if a patient expects collagen to fix a skin condition, that is a conversation for a prescriber.

In the UK, a peptide serum is a cosmetic: its responsible person needs a safety assessment and must notify the regulator before sale, and must be able to prove its claims. Oral collagen is a food supplement: no food may claim to prevent, treat or cure disease, and only authorised health claims may be used. In May 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled a peptide serum's 'clinically proven' lifting claim misleading because the study behind it was small and uncontrolled.

In the EU, a peptide serum sold as a cosmetic needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a product safety report and electronic notification to the Commission before it is placed on the market (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009), and its claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013). Food labelling and advertising may not claim that a food prevents, treats or cures a disease, and health claims on foods are prohibited unless authorised: the Commission refused a claim that a collagen peptide mixture maintains skin health by increasing elasticity and reducing wrinkles, because cause and effect was not established (Regulation (EU) No 1154/2014), and the EU Register lists no authorised claim for collagen itself (searched 25 September 2026).

In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics (Decreto-Lei 23/2025), and borderline products must be assessed case by case by the Responsible Person, taking all their characteristics into account (INFARMED, as of 25 September 2026). For food supplement notification, there is no evaluation of the product or validation of labelling; control is carried out afterwards by sampling and may take place at any time (DGAV, as of 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling must not contain trade names, brands, images, electronic links or wording that represent therapeutic claims attributed to the use of the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12). Under ANVISA's January 2025 food supplement guidance, an approved claim is that bioactive hydrolysed collagen peptides with an average molecular weight of 2 kDa help maintain skin health.

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) treats food supplements, oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease, as medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE): oral collagen products are registered with the EDE as general-sale-list health products rather than medicines, while ordinary cosmetics need a conformity certificate from the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014. Advertising any medical product, social media included, requires EDE approval. In Dubai, the DHA's rules for health facilities ban misleading or unproven peptide claims, such as anti-ageing, cell regeneration or improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status (29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, the DoH bars healthcare providers from promoting peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertising them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (31 July 2026).

Lesson three moves from the cosmetic shelf to the peptides patients buy online and inject. BPC-157 is a fifteen-residue peptide first described in 1993. Its evidence is a large rodent literature, most of it from one research group, and uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is sold as thymosin, but when anti-doping chemists analysed the product they found a seven-residue fragment, residues seventeen to twenty-three of thymosin beta-four. That fragment has never been tested in a trial. KPV is the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH; it calms inflammation in mouse colitis models, and there is no randomized human trial of it for anything. All three have plausible mechanisms, and none has a controlled human trial.

The evidence
One abstract, no published trial.

As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published in full. FDA's July 2026 briefing found one randomized, placebo-controlled trial reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, two weeks of treatment, and no significant difference from placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov adds a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, and a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff surgery due to start in 2027.

Module 05 · Opening film
Follicle, pigment and melanocortins

Two requests reach aesthetic clinics well ahead of their evidence: a peptide to regrow hair and an injection to tan. In three lessons you will see how the follicle and the pigment system run on the skin's own hormones, why one melanocortin drug is approved while its gray-market cousin is approved nowhere, and how to grade the hair peptides patients bring to you. Each hair follicle behaves like a small gland. When researchers keep human scalp follicles alive in culture, the follicles answer corticotropin-releasing hormone the way the pituitary and adrenal glands do. They make ACTH and alpha-MSH, they secrete cortisol, and cortisol-like signals feed back to switch the stimulus down. On the scalp, an enzyme called five-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, and in genetically susceptible follicles that hormone drives the gradual shrinking behind pattern hair loss. Most of this biology comes from tissue kept alive outside the body, so hold it as mechanism, a reason something might matter in patients.
Mechanism
A follicle that runs its own hormones.

Human scalp hair follicles kept alive in the laboratory answer corticotropin-releasing hormone by making ACTH and α-MSH and secreting cortisol, with a feedback loop like the adrenal axis. They also run a growth hormone and IGF-1 loop of their own. Locally made dihydrotestosterone shrinks genetically susceptible scalp follicles, the process behind pattern hair loss. Growing follicles are shielded from immune attack, and alopecia areata begins when that shield fails.
Local stress axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Local androgen switch: testosterone → DHT in the scalp
Immune privilege: its collapse drives alopecia areata
Its own stress axis
Organ-cultured human scalp follicles respond to CRH by making POMC products and secreting cortisol, and hydrocortisone in turn damps follicular CRH, the adrenal axis in miniature.
Its own growth and androgen signals
Outside the body, follicles also run a GH and IGF-1 loop. In susceptible scalp follicles, locally made DHT drives the miniaturisation of pattern hair loss.
Hidden from the immune system
Growing follicles show little antigen to immune cells. When that privilege collapses, T cells and natural killer cells attack the bulb and alopecia areata follows.

When immune privilege fails, the attack depends on cytokine signals that JAK inhibitors interrupt. Two randomized phase 3 trials tested oral baricitinib in 1,200 adults with severe alopecia areata. In the US, FDA approved baricitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata on 13 June 2022. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades it A.

Interrupting the immune signalling behind collapsed privilege regrows hair in severe alopecia areata. That is approval-grade evidence (A), and it shows what real follicle evidence looks like.

Lesson 5.2 · Concept
Five receptors, one family of hormones.

Skin makes proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and cuts it into ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. Those peptides act on five melanocortin receptors. MC1R drives pigment in skin and hair, MC2R answers ACTH in the adrenal gland, MC3R and MC4R act in the brain on appetite, and MC5R governs sebum. Which receptors a drug reaches decides what else it does.
MC1R: pigment of skin and hair
MC2R: adrenal · MC5R: sebum
MC3R and MC4R: appetite, in the brain
Made in the skin
Skin cells make POMC and cut it into ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin, and they carry the receptors that answer them.
Five receptors
MC1R pigment, MC2R adrenal, MC3R and MC4R appetite in the brain, MC5R sebum. Reviewers note the real distribution is probably wider than this tidy map.
Selectivity is the safety story
A drug that stays on MC1R mostly changes pigment. A drug that reaches the brain's receptors brings nausea, appetite loss and erections with it.

Pigment starts with hormones the skin makes for itself. Researchers caution that the real map is messier, with receptors turning up in more tissues than the textbook suggests. For this lesson one idea matters most.
