The evidence
Twenty-three trials, split by who paid.

Pooled, oral collagen trials show better hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades them C. A 2025 meta-analysis split the same kind of trials by funding and by quality. The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and low-quality trials. Unfunded and high-quality trials showed no effect.
in the 2025 meta-analysis that split oral-collagen trials by funding and quality
1,474 participants

The pooled benefit of oral collagen disappears when you look only at independent or high-quality trials. The course keeps the guide's GRADE C and shows why a downgrade has been proposed to its author.
It does not show collagen is harmful, and it does not rule out benefit for an individual. It is a statement about the evidence, and it says nothing about topical peptides.
What changes in practice
Cosmetic, supplement, drug: three rulebooks.

In the US, cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework. Oral collagen is a dietary supplement: it may not claim to treat disease, and product quality and content vary. Neither route has to prove efficacy before sale — which is why the funding question matters.
Cosmetic ingredient: no efficacy approval needed
Dietary supplement: no disease claims; quality varies
Say 'modest, small-trial' — never 'topical Botox'

Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub varies from brand to brand. That is the whole reason the funding question matters here. When no regulator asks for efficacy, the only efficacy data are the trials someone chose to pay for.
Nothing here needs a prescription. If you recommend a product, recommend it on evidence, name the grade, and disclose any relationship with the brand. The 'topical Botox' claim is not one to repeat.
When a patient asks which serum 'really works', the accurate answer is modest effects from mostly sponsor-funded trials. Do not describe any of them as an alternative to botulinum toxin.

The claim you can stand behind is modest, small-trial evidence. Supplements cannot be sold as treating a disease; if a patient expects collagen to fix a skin condition, that is a conversation for a prescriber.

In the UK, a peptide serum is a cosmetic: its responsible person needs a safety assessment and must notify the regulator before sale, and must be able to prove its claims. Oral collagen is a food supplement: no food may claim to prevent, treat or cure disease, and only authorised health claims may be used. In May 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled a peptide serum's 'clinically proven' lifting claim misleading because the study behind it was small and uncontrolled.

In the EU, a peptide serum sold as a cosmetic needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a product safety report and electronic notification to the Commission before it is placed on the market (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009), and its claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013). Food labelling and advertising may not claim that a food prevents, treats or cures a disease, and health claims on foods are prohibited unless authorised: the Commission refused a claim that a collagen peptide mixture maintains skin health by increasing elasticity and reducing wrinkles, because cause and effect was not established (Regulation (EU) No 1154/2014), and the EU Register lists no authorised claim for collagen itself (searched 25 September 2026).

In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics (Decreto-Lei 23/2025), and borderline products must be assessed case by case by the Responsible Person, taking all their characteristics into account (INFARMED, as of 25 September 2026). For food supplement notification, there is no evaluation of the product or validation of labelling; control is carried out afterwards by sampling and may take place at any time (DGAV, as of 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling must not contain trade names, brands, images, electronic links or wording that represent therapeutic claims attributed to the use of the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12). Under ANVISA's January 2025 food supplement guidance, an approved claim is that bioactive hydrolysed collagen peptides with an average molecular weight of 2 kDa help maintain skin health.

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) treats food supplements, oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease, as medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE): oral collagen products are registered with the EDE as general-sale-list health products rather than medicines, while ordinary cosmetics need a conformity certificate from the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014. Advertising any medical product, social media included, requires EDE approval. In Dubai, the DHA's rules for health facilities ban misleading or unproven peptide claims, such as anti-ageing, cell regeneration or improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status (29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, the DoH bars healthcare providers from promoting peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertising them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (31 July 2026).

Lesson 4.3 · Concept
Rodents, a fragment, and a tripeptide.

BPC-157 rests on a large rodent literature, mostly from one research group, and on uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is not thymosin β4: it is a seven-residue fragment of it, identified by analysing the product itself, and no trial has tested the fragment. KPV, a tripeptide from the end of α-MSH, calms inflammation in mouse colitis and has no randomized human trial.
BPC-157: rodents and case series
TB-500: a fragment, never trialled
KPV: mouse colitis only
BPC-157
A synthetic 15-residue peptide first described in 1993. Decades of rodent studies, most from one Zagreb group; in people, uncontrolled case series.
Sold as 'thymosin', but anti-doping chemists who analysed the product found a fragment — residues 17 to 23 — not the 43-residue parent. Ask what a patient actually bought.
KPV
The last three residues of α-MSH. Anti-inflammatory in mouse colitis models; no randomized human trials for any indication.

Lesson three moves from the cosmetic shelf to the peptides patients buy online and inject. BPC-157 is a fifteen-residue peptide first described in 1993. Its evidence is a large rodent literature, most of it from one research group, and uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is sold as thymosin, but when anti-doping chemists analysed the product they found a seven-residue fragment, residues seventeen to twenty-three of thymosin beta-four. That fragment has never been tested in a trial. KPV is the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH; it calms inflammation in mouse colitis models, and there is no randomized human trial of it for anything. All three have plausible mechanisms, and none has a controlled human trial.
A mouse on a lab plinth, a long peptide chain with a short fragment lifted out, and a shorter chain with its last three beads set apart.
The evidence
One abstract, no published trial.

As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published in full. FDA's July 2026 briefing found one randomized, placebo-controlled trial reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, two weeks of treatment, and no significant difference from placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov adds a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, and a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff surgery due to start in 2027.
randomized efficacy trials of BPC-157 in people published in full (September 2026)

One 2005 ulcerative-colitis trial exists only as a meeting abstract (no significant difference from placebo) · registered: phase 1 safety study (2015, no results) · single-arm product study (2025, no results) · randomized phase 1 after rotator-cuff repair (starts 2027)
Whether BPC-157 helps people heal is unknown. The only randomized human result is an abstract that showed no significant benefit; the enthusiasm rests on rodents and uncontrolled case series.
It does not show BPC-157 is ineffective or unsafe. Absence of trials is absence of evidence, and this figure will change when the registered trials report.

Module 05 · Opening film
Follicle, pigment and melanocortins

Two requests reach aesthetic clinics well ahead of their evidence: a peptide to regrow hair and an injection to tan. In three lessons you will see how the follicle and the pigment system run on the skin's own hormones, why one melanocortin drug is approved while its gray-market cousin is approved nowhere, and how to grade the hair peptides patients bring to you. Each hair follicle behaves like a small gland. When researchers keep human scalp follicles alive in culture, the follicles answer corticotropin-releasing hormone the way the pituitary and adrenal glands do. They make ACTH and alpha-MSH, they secrete cortisol, and cortisol-like signals feed back to switch the stimulus down. On the scalp, an enzyme called five-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, and in genetically susceptible follicles that hormone drives the gradual shrinking behind pattern hair loss. Most of this biology comes from tissue kept alive outside the body, so hold it as mechanism, a reason something might matter in patients.
Mechanism
A follicle that runs its own hormones.

Human scalp hair follicles kept alive in the laboratory answer corticotropin-releasing hormone by making ACTH and α-MSH and secreting cortisol, with a feedback loop like the adrenal axis. They also run a growth hormone and IGF-1 loop of their own. Locally made dihydrotestosterone shrinks genetically susceptible scalp follicles, the process behind pattern hair loss. Growing follicles are shielded from immune attack, and alopecia areata begins when that shield fails.
Local stress axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Local androgen switch: testosterone → DHT in the scalp
Immune privilege: its collapse drives alopecia areata
Its own stress axis
Organ-cultured human scalp follicles respond to CRH by making POMC products and secreting cortisol, and hydrocortisone in turn damps follicular CRH, the adrenal axis in miniature.
Its own growth and androgen signals
Outside the body, follicles also run a GH and IGF-1 loop. In susceptible scalp follicles, locally made DHT drives the miniaturisation of pattern hair loss.
Hidden from the immune system
Growing follicles show little antigen to immune cells. When that privilege collapses, T cells and natural killer cells attack the bulb and alopecia areata follows.

Human evidence
Two trials, 1,200 adults, one approval.

When immune privilege fails, the attack depends on cytokine signals that JAK inhibitors interrupt. Two randomized phase 3 trials tested oral baricitinib in 1,200 adults with severe alopecia areata. In the US, FDA approved baricitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata on 13 June 2022. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades it A.
adults with severe alopecia areata in the two phase 3 trials of baricitinib (2022)
At 36 weeks, up to 39% of patients on baricitinib had at least 80% of their scalp hair, against 3–6% on placebo
Interrupting the immune signalling behind collapsed privilege regrows hair in severe alopecia areata. That is approval-grade evidence (A), and it shows what real follicle evidence looks like.
It says nothing about pattern hair loss, cosmetic thinning or any peptide. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer, and the authors called for longer trials.
In the UK, baricitinib is licensed for severe alopecia areata in adults, and NICE did not recommend it for NHS use in October 2023, on cost-effectiveness.

In the EU, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been centrally authorised since 13 February 2017; its indications include severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over, and it is prescription-only, started by a doctor experienced in the condition (EMA). Since EMA's January 2023 review, JAK inhibitors including Olumiant should be used in people aged 65 or over, at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk, or long-term smokers only if no suitable alternative exists, and this applies to alopecia areata.
In Portugal, Olumiant (baricitinib) is classified as a restricted-prescription medicine (MSRM restrita - Alínea a), according to INFARMED's Infomed register on 25 September 2026.

In Brazil, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been registered by ANVISA since 26 November 2018, and its current label includes severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 or over weighing at least 30 kg (checked 25 September 2026).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. The EDE register lists Olumiant (baricitinib) tablets, registered since 8 June 2017, as Prescription Only and files them under rheumatic diseases; it does not show whether alopecia areata is an approved UAE indication (25 September 2026).

Lesson 5.2 · Concept
Five receptors, one family of hormones.

Skin makes proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and cuts it into ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. Those peptides act on five melanocortin receptors. MC1R drives pigment in skin and hair, MC2R answers ACTH in the adrenal gland, MC3R and MC4R act in the brain on appetite, and MC5R governs sebum. Which receptors a drug reaches decides what else it does.
MC1R: pigment of skin and hair
MC2R: adrenal · MC5R: sebum

Pigment starts with hormones the skin makes for itself. Skin cells produce a precursor called POMC and cut it into ACTH, alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. There are five melanocortin receptors. MC1R sets the pigment of skin and hair. MC2R is the adrenal receptor for ACTH. MC3R and MC4R work in the brain on appetite, and central receptors also drive sexual responses. MC5R governs sebum. Researchers caution that the real map is messier, with receptors turning up in more tissues than the textbook suggests. For this lesson one idea matters most. A drug that stays on MC1R mostly changes pigment, and a drug that reaches the brain's receptors brings other effects with it.

Afamelanotide and Melanotan II are both synthetic relatives of α-MSH. Compare them register by register and the resemblance ends at the receptor.

Two phase 3 trials in erythropoietic protoporphyria, against a three-volunteer pilot and a ten-man erectile-dysfunction study from the 1990s. The Peptide Pocket Guide rates Melanotan II C and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide D; with no trial of tanning, this course uses D.

In the UK, afamelanotide is licensed under exceptional circumstances and prescribed only in specialist porphyria centres, and NICE did not recommend it for NHS use (July 2023).

In the EU, afamelanotide (Scenesse implant) is authorised for erythropoietic protoporphyria, under exceptional circumstances (European Commission, 22 December 2014), and is prescribed only by specialists in recognised EPP centres.

In Portugal, Scenesse is authorised through the EU procedure but classified as a restricted-prescription medicine for exclusive hospital use (MSRM restrita, alínea a), and no presentation is marketed in Portugal (INFARMED's Infomed register, 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing afamelanotide (Scenesse) was found: ANVISA's open-data register and its online medicines search returned no match on 25 September 2026, and the substance is absent from ANVISA's substance dictionary.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. The evidence
Sixty-nine hours against forty-one.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is a rare disorder in which sunlight causes acute, severe pain. In the US phase 3 trial, adults on afamelanotide spent a median 69.4 hours in direct sunlight without pain over six months, against 40.8 hours on placebo. The European trial also showed more pain-free time and fewer phototoxic reactions. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer.
median pain-free hours in direct sunlight over six months, afamelanotide vs placebo (US phase 3 trial, 94 adults with EPP)
Langendonk et al., NEJM 2015 · European trial, 74 adults: 6.0 vs 0.8 hours over nine months
Afamelanotide lets people with EPP spend more time in sunlight without pain. That is approval-grade evidence (A) for one rare disease.
It says nothing about cosmetic tanning, about Melanotan II, or about unsupervised injections. Even in EPP, the US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice a year.
Safety signals
What the case reports show.

The harms of Melanotan II come from case reports and reviews, so they show what can happen without telling you how often. Reported skin effects include darkening and growth of existing moles, crops of new and sometimes atypical naevi, and dark bands in the nails. At least five melanomas have been reported during or after use, each in someone with other risk factors, so causation is unproven. Systemic reports include ischaemic priapism needing surgery and a stimulant-like toxic reaction with rhabdomyolysis, and FDA lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious events.

Melanoma: reported, causation unproven
Systemic: priapism, rhabdomyolysis, encephalopathy
Moles and nails
Existing moles darken and grow, new naevi appear in crops, some atypical on histology, and nails can develop dark bands. In one report the new naevi faded after the injections stopped.
Melanoma, a signal without proof
At least five melanomas have been reported during or after use. Every patient had other risk factors, such as fair skin, sunbed use or a family history.
The rest of the body
Nausea, flushing and yawning are common. Reported emergencies include ischaemic priapism needing surgery, rhabdomyolysis with kidney injury, and encephalopathy.

Now the harms, and the kind of evidence behind them. Everything here comes from case reports and reviews, which tell you what can happen and leave open how often it does. In the skin, existing moles darken and grow, new moles erupt in crops, some of them atypical under the microscope, and dark bands can appear in the nails. At least five melanomas have been reported during or after Melanotan use. Each patient had other risk factors, such as fair skin, sunbed use or a family history, so causation is unproven, and the concern rests on a drug that pushes melanocytes to multiply. Beyond the skin, reports describe priapism that needed surgery, a stimulant-like toxic reaction with muscle breakdown and kidney injury, and a brain swelling syndrome that FDA lists among the published serious events.

Lesson 5.3 · Concept
A Wnt switch and a zinc question.

PTD-DBM joins a cell-penetrating peptide to a short decoy sequence that stops the protein CXXC5 from binding Dishevelled. Freed from that brake, Wnt/β-catenin signalling rises, and in mice hair regrew faster. Its developers also found CXXC5 raised in human balding scalp. Zinc thymulin is a thymic peptide that is active only when bound to zinc. How it might act on hair has never been defined, and whether any effect would come from the peptide or the zinc is unknown.
PTD-DBM: releases a Wnt brake (mouse data)
Zinc thymulin: a zinc-dependent thymic peptide
Both: mechanism first, human data absent
PTD-DBM
A cell-penetrating tag carries a decoy sequence into follicle cells. The decoy keeps CXXC5 off Dishevelled, so Wnt signalling can rise.
What was shown
Faster hair regrowth, and new follicles in healed wounds, in mice. The work came from the developer's own group, which also found CXXC5 raised in human balding scalp tissue.
Zinc thymulin
A thymic hormone that works only with zinc bound. Its proposed hair effect has no defined mechanism and no indexed human study.

Two peptides are sold for hair, and both arrive with better stories than data. PTD-DBM joins a cell-penetrating fragment borrowed from an HIV protein to a short decoy sequence. Inside follicle cells, the decoy keeps a protein called CXXC5 from binding its partner, Dishevelled, and that releases a brake on Wnt signalling, a pathway involved in hair regrowth. In mice, hair regrew faster and follicles formed in healed wounds. The work came from the developer's own group. Zinc thymulin is a thymic hormone that becomes active only when zinc binds to it. How it might help hair has never been defined, and nobody has shown whether any effect would come from the peptide or from the zinc. Hold both as mechanism, and look for the human trial.
Inside a cell, a small decoy peptide keeps a brake protein from docking on a signalling protein, and small signal tokens move into the nucleus.
The evidence
Zero trials in people.

As of September 2026, PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov list no human trial of PTD-DBM, published or registered. Its evidence is one 2017 study in mice and human scalp tissue from the developer's group, whose senior author is affiliated with a biotech company. A 2025 review's summary speaks of 'clinical efficacy', yet the review's own text describes PTD-DBM results in mouse models only.
human trials of PTD-DBM, published or registered (September 2026)
Lee et al., J Invest Dermatol 2017: mice, plus CXXC5 measured in human scalp tissue
Whether PTD-DBM regrows human hair is unknown. The Peptide Pocket Guide and this course grade it D.

It does not show that PTD-DBM fails or harms. One open safety question sits alongside: the 2025 review flags that off-target Wnt activation is associated with colorectal and liver cancers, a theoretical concern nobody has tested for this peptide.

Stated for the United States, the regulatory picture is short. On FDA's category lists of the fourteenth of May, twenty twenty-six, thymulin acetate sits in Category 3, meaning it was nominated without enough information for FDA to evaluate, and it falls outside the enforcement discretion that Category 1 substances receive. In the UK, a spray made up for one patient would be an unlicensed 'special', and MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed one, such as minoxidil, could meet the patient's need.

In the EU, a medicine prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (a magistral formula) falls outside Directive 2001/83/EC (Article 3). A search of the Union Register and EMA's medicines data found no centrally authorised medicine containing thymulin or PTD-DBM (25 September 2026).

In Portugal, a magistral formula may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia or compendial scientific documentation, and the prescribing physician must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy (Decreto-Lei 95/2004). INFARMED's Infomed register lists no medicine containing thymulin or PTD-DBM (25 September 2026).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that a substance must have passed efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded, and that compounding may only be individual, on prescription, by a pharmacy licensed by local health surveillance. A search of ANVISA's register found no registered medicine containing PTD-DBM or thymulin (25 September 2026), though immunomodulators such as thymomodulin are registered.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023; under the medicines law, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies need no marketing approval, and no product containing thymulin or PTD-DBM was found in the EDE register (25 September 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the Department of Health (DoH) lets compounded peptide formulations use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight (31 July 2026), and its August 2026 compounding standard treats peptides as emerging, high-risk substances that may be compounded only if monographed, part of an approved medicine or listed on the DoH's register of compounded substances.

Module 06 · Opening film
The growth-hormone axis and the skin

Growth hormone and IGF-1 genuinely shape skin, and one peptide on this axis has approval-grade trials. Most of what patients are offered has much less behind it. In three lessons you will separate the physiology from the promise, the approved from the anecdotal, and the side-effects you can see from the risks nobody has measured. Two layers of skin listen to two different parts of the same axis. Growth hormone speaks mainly to the dermis. Its receptor is expressed more on fibroblasts than on keratinocytes, and in culture growth hormone increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis, sometimes directly and sometimes through IGF-1. The epidermis listens to IGF-1. Keratinocytes carry the IGF-1 receptor, their neighbours in the dermis supply the hormone, and in culture IGF-1 makes keratinocytes divide where growth hormone on its own does nothing. With age, growth-hormone pulses and IGF-1 fall steadily, a change called the somatopause. Hold all of this as mechanism. It explains why the axis could matter for skin. Whether changing it helps a patient is a separate question, and the trials answer it.
Lesson 6.1 · Mechanism
Two hormones, two layers of skin.

Growth hormone acts mostly in the dermis. Its receptor is expressed more by fibroblasts than by keratinocytes, and it increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, reaches keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor and makes them divide. Human hair follicles even run their own small growth-hormone loop in the laboratory. With age, GH secretion and IGF-1 fall steadily; this is the somatopause.
GH: dermal fibroblasts and collagen
IGF-1: keratinocyte proliferation, supplied locally
Somatopause: GH and IGF-1 fall with age
The dermis listens to GH
Growth-hormone receptors sit mainly on dermal fibroblasts. GH, directly or through IGF-1, supports fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis.
The epidermis listens to IGF-1
Keratinocytes carry the IGF-1 receptor but make little IGF-1 themselves; fibroblasts supply it. In culture, IGF-1 makes keratinocytes divide and GH on its own does not.
The axis ages
GH pulses and IGF-1 fall from early adulthood. Reference ranges are age-adjusted, so an IGF-1 that is low for a 25-year-old is often normal for the patient's age.

Human evidence
A much-cited skin result, read again.

In 1990 a much-cited New England Journal of Medicine study gave growth hormone for six months to 12 healthy men over 60, with nine untreated men for comparison and no placebo. Lean mass rose and fat fell. Skin thickness rose 7.1%, with P = 0.07, short of statistical significance. A small 1996 randomized trial in 28 older men found 15% more collagen laid down in implanted wound tubes on GH, a laboratory surrogate for repair.
rise in skin thickness in 12 older men given growth hormone for six months (1990)
P = 0.07 · nine untreated men as comparison · no placebo
A skin result still quoted for growth hormone comes from 12 treated men, without a placebo, and it missed statistical significance. Graded on its design, it is D.
It does not show that GH thins skin or that it fails in true deficiency, and it says nothing about secretagogues. It shows how thin the direct skin evidence for growth hormone in healthy ageing is.

What changes in practice
Deficiency is a diagnosis. Decline is ageing.

In healthy older adults, randomized trials of growth hormone show small shifts in body composition, about 2 kg less fat and 2 kg more lean mass, with more oedema, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and a trend towards diabetes. Strength and endurance change little. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades its advice against treatment A; graded on the trials themselves the evidence is B, and the conclusion is the same. In the US, as of September 2026, knowingly distributing growth hormone for anti-ageing is a federal offence.
Healthy ageing: small body-composition change, more side-effects
Grade B on the trials (guide: A), same conclusion
US: anti-ageing distribution is a federal offence
What the trials show
Pooled randomized trials in healthy older adults: about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass, weight unchanged.
What they cost
More soft-tissue oedema, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia, and a trend towards diabetes. In one trial, 39% of women on GH developed oedema, against none on placebo.
Where it stands
Growth hormone is for diagnosed deficiency and a short list of approved conditions. In the US, distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence.

Here the physiology meets the waiting room. A patient in their fifties has read that growth hormone falls with age and asks whether topping it up would help their skin. The trials in healthy older adults answer that. Pooled, they show about two kilograms less fat and two kilograms more lean mass, with more swelling, joint pain, carpal tunnel symptoms and a drift towards diabetes, while strength and stamina change little. Graded on those trials the evidence is B, consistent and independent though small, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide gives its advice against treatment an A. Both land in the same place. Growth hormone treats a diagnosed deficiency and a short list of approved conditions. In the United States, distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence. Whatever your role, name the decline for what it is, a normal part of ageing.

Prescribe growth hormone only for a confirmed deficiency or another approved indication, usually with an endocrinologist. For a request framed as anti-ageing, document the conversation, the evidence you quoted and the legal position, and decline.
If a patient mentions growth hormone or 'HGH' for skin or energy, record what they use, where it comes from and any swelling, joint pain or tingling, and bring it to the prescriber.

You can explain that growth hormone falls normally with age and that trials in healthy adults show more side-effects than benefit. Anyone who wants to start it needs a prescriber's assessment rather than a product recommendation.
In the UK, somatropin is a prescription-only medicine licensed for growth hormone deficiency and specific growth disorders, and a Class C controlled drug.

In the EU, somatropin medicines have been authorised since the 1980s, through central and national procedures, for growth hormone replacement and for short stature in specific childhood conditions (EMA, 2012). The centrally authorised Omnitrope (since 12 April 2006) is prescription-only, and treatment is started and monitored by a doctor experienced in growth disorders.

In Portugal, somatropin medicines are authorised as restricted-prescription medicines, reserved for conditions diagnosed only in hospital or specialised settings, and INFARMED's register gives them no narcotic classification (25 September 2026). Growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services, and a national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for its administration.

In Brazil, somatropin is registered for replacement therapy in adults with marked growth hormone deficiency, and it is a controlled substance on List C5 (anabolic substances) that needs a special-control prescription in two copies (RDC 1.036/2026). The Federal Council of Medicine's Resolution 1.999/2012, in force in September 2026, bars the use of hormones, including growth hormone, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023; the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, which prohibits advertising semi-controlled products to the public. Somatropin is registered with the EDE and is on the federal list of semi-controlled medical products (MOHAP Ministerial Decision 306/2023), and every somatropin entry in the EDE register is dispensed as a semi-controlled drug (25 September 2026).

Lesson 6.2 · Concept
One axis, four ways in.

Somatropin is growth hormone itself. GHRH analogues (sermorelin, tesamorelin, CJC-1295) stimulate the pituitary's GHRH receptor. Ghrelin-receptor agonists (ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and the oral ibutamoren, MK-677) stimulate GH release through a second pituitary receptor. IGF-1 analogues such as IGF-1 LR3 bypass the pituitary altogether. They are sold as one family, and the next moments take them apart.
Replace: somatropin
Stimulate: GHRH analogues and ghrelin-receptor agonists
Bypass: IGF-1 analogues
Replace
Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone. It replaces the hormone itself.
Stimulate
GHRH analogues and ghrelin-receptor agonists push the patient's own pituitary to release growth hormone, in pulses.
Bypass
IGF-1 analogues act directly on the IGF-1 receptor, downstream of the pituitary.

Four routes lead into the same axis, and patients rarely know which one they are on. Somatropin is growth hormone itself, made by recombinant technology. GHRH analogues, sermorelin, tesamorelin and CJC-1295, press on the pituitary's releasing-hormone receptor, so the gland releases its own growth hormone in pulses. Ghrelin-receptor agonists, ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and the oral compound ibutamoren, press on a second pituitary receptor. IGF-1 analogues such as IGF-1 LR3 skip the pituitary and act on the IGF-1 receptor directly. Every route ends at that same receptor, which is why lesson three treats their risks together. Clinics often sell all of these as one family with one promise. Keep them apart, because the trials, the approvals and the side-effects belong to each molecule separately.

The evidence
Zero skin trials.

A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3. The nearest is a 1997 study of a GHRH(1-29) analogue related to sermorelin, in 19 older adults. Skin thickness measured by caliper rose after 16 weeks, compared with a placebo lead-in rather than a parallel control group.

Tesamorelin is the only GHRH analogue with a current FDA-approved indication, and it is not a skin treatment. Do not prescribe compounded secretagogues on the strength of a mechanism; document what the patient uses and assess or refer any sign of GH excess.
Ask which product, from whom and for how long, and record the exact name on the vial. Report swelling, tingling, joint pain or new skin changes to the prescriber. Do not advise on amounts or timing.

Describe these products accurately: one approved use for tesamorelin, hormone-level data or nothing for the rest, and no US bulks-list standing for the secretagogues. Refer anyone injecting them to a prescriber.

In the UK, MHRA's products database holds no product information for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin (searched 25 September 2026), so any of them would reach a patient only as an unlicensed medicine. An unlicensed special needs a clinical need that no licensed medicine meets.

In the EU, tesamorelin has no marketing authorisation (its application was withdrawn on 21 June 2012), and no centrally authorised medicine containing sermorelin or ipamorelin was found in the Union Register or EMA's data (25 September 2026). EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, no medicine containing tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin is listed in INFARMED's Infomed register, which includes authorised, lapsed and revoked products (25 September 2026). INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento).

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing tesamorelin or sermorelin was found in ANVISA's register (25 September 2026). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides called ipamorelin that promise aesthetic effects or health improvements are not registered with ANVISA, and that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category and are therefore illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023; the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. No registered product containing tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin was found in the EDE register (25 September 2026). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits prescribing, dispensing or using any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and bans misleading or unproven anti-ageing claims for peptides (29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status (DoH, 31 July 2026).

Whether it raises IGF-1
A higher IGF-1 is a laboratory result. Benefit to a patient needs a clinical trial. First, which molecule, exactly.
Whether other patients' skin improved on it
Every skin promise made for these peptides rests on mechanism and anecdote. First, which molecule, exactly.
It is 'Mod GRF 1-29': CJC-1295 without DAC. What stands behind it?

That is CJC-1295 with DAC: two phase 1 trials in healthy adults showed GH and IGF-1 rising for days, and neither measured a clinical outcome. Only the DAC form has been given to people in a trial.

Lesson 6.3 · Recognition
What too much growth hormone looks like.

Sustained GH excess changes skin in ways you can see. In acromegaly, glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema make the face, hands and feet puffy and thick; the skin turns oily with large pores; sweating increases; skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear. Drugs on this axis bring their own signs: fluid retention with swelling, joint pain, tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. The Endocrine Society recommends measuring IGF-1 when typical acral and facial features are present.
Soft tissue: puffy, thickened face, hands and feet
Skin: oily, sweaty, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans
On treatment: swelling, joint pain, tingling
In the skin
Glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema thicken the skin of the face, hands and feet. Skin turns oily, pores enlarge, sweating increases, and skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear.
In the soft tissues
Hands and feet enlarge slowly and the jaw widens. On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention brings swelling, joint pain and night-time tingling.
When to test

The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 for typical acral and facial features, and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster, including sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis and hypertension.

Excess growth hormone leaves visible marks on skin and soft tissue, and noticing them early matters. In acromegaly, glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema thicken the face, hands and feet, so features look puffy and coarse. The skin turns oily with large pores, sweating increases, and skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear. Hands and feet enlarge slowly, and the jaw widens. Drugs on this axis bring their own signs, usually transient, with swelling, joint pain, tingling fingers and carpal tunnel symptoms. On somatropin, the label asks for existing moles to be watched for growth or malignant change. The Endocrine Society recommends measuring IGF-1 when typical acral and facial features are present, and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster. For most of you the job is recognition and referral, and the diagnosis belongs to endocrinology.

Four registers
Does raising IGF-1 cause cancer?
The honest answer has four parts, and each has its own source. Keep them apart, or a mechanism will be heard as a measured risk.
Mechanism
Plausible
IGF-1 receptor signalling drives cell proliferation and survival, which gives any IGF-1-raising product a theoretical concern
Human observation
Modest associations

In large studies, higher natural IGF-1 goes with slightly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer; reverse causation is not excluded. In one Ecuadorian cohort, people with GH-receptor deficiency had almost no cancer.
Acromegaly
Slightly raised, inconsistently
Pooled studies show about 1.5 times the expected cancer incidence, with the highest estimates from small single-centre series; a Danish nationwide cohort found no clear rise
GH replacement
Largely reassuring
No clear raised risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other disease; a 2022 consensus found no link with primary tumours or recurrence in survivors
Open question
Unmeasured
No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin
A plausible mechanism plus a modest association is a reason for caution and consent. It is a different thing from a measured risk.
The evidence
Half the patients on the approved one.

Tesamorelin is the best-studied peptide on this axis. In its pivotal trials, 47% of treated patients had IGF-1 more than two standard deviations above the mean at 26 weeks, and 36% more than three. Its label states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown. For unapproved secretagogues bought for skin, nobody has published the equivalent figure.
of tesamorelin-treated patients with IGF-1 above +2 SD at 26 weeks in its pivotal trials
36% above +3 SD · label: effects of prolonged elevation unknown
Pushing IGF-1 above the normal range is common even with an approved GHRH analogue used as labelled, in monitored trials.
It does not show that tesamorelin causes cancer, and it is no target to aim for. It shows why sustained, unmonitored use of any IGF-1-raising product is an open safety question.

Physiology or promise?
A fictional clinic page for a growth-hormone peptide. Find the lines the evidence does not support.
Growth hormone and IGF-1 fall steadily from early adulthood.
Sound. GH pulses and IGF-1 fall from early adulthood: the somatopause, a normal part of ageing.

Evidence, regulation and compliance

This last module turns the course into three habits. You will rate the certainty behind a claim with GRADE, read a compounding status and a certificate of analysis for what they do and do not prove, and write the consent and chart note that an unapproved product needs. Every claim you hear about a skin peptide carries a hidden question. How sure can we be? GRADE answers it with four levels of certainty, from high to very low. The rating belongs to a body of evidence for one outcome, such as wrinkle depth at twelve weeks, and never to a single study or to the molecule itself. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low. From there, certainty drops for five reasons you can name, which are risk of bias, inconsistency between trials, indirectness, imprecision, and suspected publication bias. Both Hormonaly guides print a letter from A to D beside each use. Read those letters as the same four levels, adapted. They rate the evidence for that use, and they say nothing about whether a product is legal.
Lesson 7.1 · Concept
GRADE rates certainty in an effect, one outcome at a time.

GRADE sorts the evidence on a specific question into four levels of certainty: high, moderate, low and very low. The rating applies to a body of evidence for one outcome, never to a single study or to a molecule. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; certainty then falls for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias, and occasionally rises for a very large effect. Both Hormonaly guides print the letters A to D for the same idea, adapted, and attach each letter to a specific use.
Four levels, applied to a body of evidence
Five named reasons to rate down
The letter belongs to a use, never to a molecule
Four levels
High, moderate, low, very low: how confident you can be that an estimated effect is close to the truth, for one outcome, across all the studies that address it.
Where you start
Randomized trials start at high certainty and observational studies at low. The starting point then moves, for reasons you can name.
The guides' letters
A to D in both Hormonaly guides maps onto the same four levels. The letter rates the evidence for a listed use. It does not rate legality, popularity or mechanism.

Four shelves of certainty: randomized trials start on the top shelf with one dot stepping down, observational studies lie on the third shelf, and a small cluster rests on the lowest.
Who paid
Sponsored studies come out better.

A Cochrane methodology review brought together 75 papers, each comparing studies sponsored by the manufacturer with studies funded in other ways. Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results and favourable conclusions, and the difference was not explained by the usual risk-of-bias checks. It is the pattern you met with oral collagen in module 04.
risk ratio for a favourable efficacy result, industry-sponsored versus other studies
Lundh et al., Cochrane 2017 · 95% CI 1.17–1.37 · moderate-certainty evidence
When a manufacturer pays for the trial, a favourable result is more likely. Funding is a reason to read a trial harder and to look for independent replication.
It does not make a sponsored trial wrong or an independent one right. It describes an average tilt across many studies and says nothing about any single product.
Worked example
Name what lowers certainty.

GRADE names the ways a body of evidence can mislead. Read the four you will use most. Then sort four cases from this course by the reason that most lowers certainty. The fifth, publication bias, is suspected when the evidence is a handful of small, mostly commercially funded studies.
Risk of bias
How the trials were run
Flaws in design or conduct that can exaggerate an effect; check whether low- and high-quality trials disagree
Inconsistency
The trials disagree
Unexplained differences in results between studies of the same question
Indirectness
A different question answered
The studies differ from your question in population, intervention, comparison or outcome
Imprecision
Too little data
Too few people or events; the confidence interval spans an important effect and little or none
Name the reason and you can explain a grade to a patient in one sentence.

One case at a time: which reason most lowers certainty here?
Risk of bias
Inconsistency

What changes in practice
Two checks, never one.

Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate axes, and both Hormonaly guides ask you to clear both. An approved drug can carry a low grade for the use a patient wants, and a compound with stronger human data can still have no lawful route. A plausible mechanism never raises a grade. Say the outcome, the grade and who ran the trials, then check the status as its own step.
Grade: certainty for this outcome
Status: what the law allows, checked separately
Mechanism never raises a grade
Start with the outcome

Mechanism
A persuasive mechanism leaves the grade where it is. Both Hormonaly guides say so in almost the same words.

Suppose a patient asks whether a peptide works. Start with the outcome they care about, say fewer lines around the eyes, and give the certainty for that outcome, along with who paid for the trials behind it. Then, as a separate step, check what the product legally is. The Hormonaly guides keep these two checks apart for a reason. An approved drug can carry a low grade for the particular use a patient has in mind, and a compound with stronger human data may still have no lawful route in the United States. A persuasive mechanism leaves the grade exactly where it is. Whatever your role, say the outcome and the grade in one breath, and treat the regulatory answer as a question of its own.

Before you recommend or prescribe, write the outcome and its grade in the note, and record the product's regulatory status on a separate line. If no trial addresses the outcome the patient wants, say so and record it.

Lesson 7.2 · Concept
Two compounding routes, one strict order.

In the US, section 503A lets a licensed pharmacist or physician compound for an identified patient on a prescription, exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and good manufacturing practice. The bulk substance must meet a USP or NF monograph; failing that, be a component of an approved drug; failing that, appear on FDA's 503A bulks list. It must also come from an FDA-registered establishment with a valid certificate of analysis. Section 503B outsourcing facilities register with FDA, work to good manufacturing practice under inspection, and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions.
503A: patient-specific, three exemptions
Monograph, then approved component, then the bulks list
503B: registered, inspected, held to good manufacturing practice

A licensed pharmacist or physician compounds for an identified patient on a valid prescription. Meeting the conditions exempts the product from approval, adequate directions and good manufacturing practice, and from nothing else.
The order of routes

Monograph first. Only if none exists, a component of an approved drug. Only if neither applies, the 503A bulks list. A valid certificate of analysis and a registered manufacturer are conditions as well.
Outsourcing facilities register with FDA, meet good manufacturing practice, are inspected on a risk-based schedule and report adverse events. Their products remain unapproved.

Two routes exist for compounding in the United States, and the difference between them shapes the rest of this lesson. Under section 503A, a licensed pharmacist or physician prepares a drug for an identified patient on a prescription. If the conditions are met, the product escapes three requirements, namely approval as a new drug, labelling with adequate directions, and good manufacturing practice. The conditions start with the substance itself, taken in strict order. A USP or National Formulary monograph comes first. Only when there is none can it be a component of an approved drug, and only when neither applies can it sit on FDA's 503A bulks list. The substance must also come from a registered manufacturer with a valid certificate of analysis. Section 503B outsourcing facilities work differently. They register with FDA, work to good manufacturing practice, face risk-based inspection, and can compound without a prescription for each patient. Their products remain unapproved.

In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formulas) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formulas) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC (Article 3). Pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies are also exempt from manufacturing authorisation (Article 40(2)).

In Portugal, a magistral formula is prepared in a community or hospital pharmacy on a medical prescription naming the patient, under a pharmacist's responsibility (Decreto-Lei 95/2004). Compounded medicines may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia or compendial scientific documentation, and one containing any other raw material may not be prescribed.

In Brazil, a magistral preparation is made individually by a pharmacy against a prescription from an authorised professional (RDC 96/2008). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that any substance must have passed efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded, and that compounding may take place only individually, on a medical prescription, in a pharmacy licensed by local health surveillance.

In the UAE, where the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has regulated medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies are exempt from marketing approval under Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 (Art. 5(2)), although such a pharmacy may not copy an EDE-approved product unless no commercial product can deliver the expected benefit, nor formulate products for research, development or experimentation (Art. 95). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) treats peptides as high-risk substances and lets novel substances of unknown risk be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits prescribing, dispensing or using any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026).

In the UAE, no registered product containing BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, LL-37, GHK-Cu or melanotan was found in the register of the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (searched 25 September 2026). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026). Peptide or biologic
Forty amino acids.

Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, whether or not it is chemically synthesized, so anything above the line is a biological product. On that date tesamorelin, a 44-residue GHRH analogue, and the enzyme hyaluronidase moved to biologics licences, and FDA told compounders that transitioned biologics cannot use the 503A or 503B exemptions.
amino acids: above this, FDA treats the molecule as a protein, and so as a biological product

Size decides the rulebook. Peptides of 40 or fewer alpha amino acids stay drugs, so the 503A questions apply; above 40 the product is a biologic, and the compounding exemptions are closed to it.

It does not make a short peptide lawful to compound; BPC-157 (15 residues) and GHK (3) still need a 503A route. How residues are counted can be contested: a court upheld FDA's count of 39 for retatrutide in 2025, and the appeal was still open at the latest filings (June 2026).

In the EU, tesamorelin has no marketing authorisation: the application for Egrifta, for excess abdominal fat in HIV patients with lipodystrophy, was withdrawn on 21 June 2012, when the provisional view of EMA's human-medicines committee (CHMP) was that it could not be approved.
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing tesamorelin, including Egrifta, was found in ANVISA's register or online search (25 September 2026).

In the UAE, no registered product containing tesamorelin, and none named Egrifta, was found in the register of the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (searched 25 September 2026).
Regulatory status (outside the US)
Outside the US, 503A does not apply.

FDA's 503A bulks list and its categories are US law and policy and apply only in the US. In the other jurisdictions in this course, a medicine without a marketing authorisation reaches a patient as a pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply made on a prescription, and the prescriber answers for that choice.
FDA's bulks list and categories
US only
Set under US federal law and FDA policy; no other jurisdiction in this course applies them.
The route
A pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply
Made or supplied on a prescription, for a product with no marketing authorisation in that jurisdiction.
Responsibility
The prescriber's
The prescriber answers for choosing a medicine without a marketing authorisation.
A 503A category means nothing outside the US: name the route your own law provides, and check it on the day.

The UK handles unlicensed medicines by a different route. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may be supplied to meet one patient's special needs, made to a prescriber's specification by a manufacturer that holds a specials licence, and it may not be advertised. The route (regulation 167): One patient, one prescriber, an unsolicited order. Made to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under their direct care. No advertisement may be published. Who makes it: A manufacturer with a specials licence. The site is inspected for good manufacturing practice; the product itself is otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy. A pharmacist may also prepare a medicine in a registered pharmacy against a prescription. Special need: The patient's clinical need. MHRA's examples include an intolerance or allergy to an ingredient, or an inability to swallow solid doses. Cost, convenience and operational needs do not count. MHRA's order of preference: Licensed, then off-label, then imported, then special. A UK-licensed medicine comes first, even used off-label; then one licensed in its country of origin; then a UK special. Least acceptable are products that are not medicines where they are made, such as supplements. Responsibility: The prescriber's. Be satisfied the evidence supports safety and efficacy, take responsibility for the prescription and the follow-up, record your reasons, and explain them to the patient when the use is not routine. GMC, MHRA and GPhC guidance say this; nurse prescribers work within the NMC Code. Cost and convenience never justify a special, and a licensed option that meets the need comes first. Dated to the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 and MHRA guidance as read on 25 September 2026.

In the EU, a member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)). Medicines prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formulas) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formulas) are outside the Directive and need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).

In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 July 2011), but it may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento). A physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004).

In Brazil, unregistered medicines may be imported only exceptionally, for strictly personal use and on a medical prescription, and import by any route is suspended when ANVISA publishes a specific prohibition; ANVISA stated in September 2025 that using an unregistered imported medicine is entirely the responsibility of the patient and the prescribing physician. ANVISA also stated in November 2024 that compounded medicines should be used only when the registered industrial product is unavailable in the dose or dosage form the patient needs.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 exempts products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies from marketing approval (Art. 5(2)) and lets a physician prescribe a product never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval only when necessary, with no equivalent alternative available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and where permitted it limits prescribing to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and dispensing by compounding pharmacies to individual prescriptions. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026).
Concept
What a certificate can and cannot prove.

A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own report on a named lot. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. HPLC gives purity as a percentage, which says nothing about what the impurities are. Endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results complete it. A certificate cannot prove that the vial in your hand came from that lot, how it was stored since, or that it is sterile and suitable to inject.
Identity: mass spectrometry, observed against expected
Purity: an HPLC percentage, impurities unnamed
Suitability to inject needs sterility, endotoxin and the right lot
Identity

Mass spectrometry confirms the molecule's mass. A serious certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. In one seized vial, high-resolution mass spectrometry found an undocumented analogue of a known peptide.
Purity
HPLC gives the main peak as a percentage. When FDA's reviewers looked at public BPC-157 certificates, most reported purity alone, with no impurity limits.
Endotoxin

The acceptable endotoxin level is calculated from the product's dose and route, so a figure without that context proves little. The certificate a BPC-157 nominator sent FDA mentioned no endotoxin test.

Picture the certificate a patient hands you, and read it line by line, asking what each line actually tests. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate shows the expected mass next to the one measured. HPLC reports purity as a percentage of the main peak, which tells you how much else is present and nothing about what that something else is. Endotoxin matters for anything injected, and FDA's guidance says the acceptable limit is calculated from the dose and the route, so a bare figure settles little. When FDA reviewed BPC-157 for its advisory committee, most public certificates listed purity alone, and the one a nominator supplied mentioned no endotoxin test. Then remember what paper cannot do. A certificate describes a lot. It cannot show that your vial came from that lot, how the vial was stored, or that it is sterile.

Label against laboratory
99% on the label.

Researchers made test purchases of semaglutide from illegal online pharmacies and analysed what arrived. The three vials that were delivered were all judged probably substandard or falsified: purity measured 7.7–14.4% against the 99% printed on the label, peptide content ran 29–39% above the labelled amount, and endotoxin was found in every vial, although none grew microorganisms.

Purity printed on a label can be wildly wrong, and a vial that grows nothing can still carry endotoxin. Independent testing found what the paperwork hid.

Three vials of one drug give no market-wide failure rate, and semaglutide is outside the skin-peptide shelf. It documents the gap between claim and content for one product; it does not measure research peptides as a class.
What changes in practice
Research use only is a label, and never a route.

In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling lets a supplier ship an investigational drug for laboratory or in-vitro research, and obliges the shipper to check that is how it will be used. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions. A certificate cannot turn such a product into a pharmaceutical.
The label permits laboratory research only
Intended use is read from how a product is sold
A certificate cannot convert a research product
A shipping permission
The US rule lets a supplier ship a drug for laboratory or in-vitro research when the label says it is not for use in humans.
Intended use
FDA reads what a product is for from its claims, marketing and how it is sold, so a disclaimer on a vial sold for injection carries no weight.
The certificate
However clean, it cannot supply sterility, manufacturing standards or a lawful route.

Research use only sounds like a category. In law it works as a shipping permission. The US rule lets a supplier send an investigational drug for laboratory or test-tube work if the label says it must stay out of people, and the shipper is meant to confirm that is how it will be used. FDA judges what a product is for by how it is marketed and sold, so a disclaimer on a vial offered with injection instructions carries no weight. The Hormonaly guides say it plainly. Research use only is not a clinical pathway. A certificate of analysis, however clean, cannot convert that vial into a pharmaceutical, because sterility, manufacturing standards and a lawful route are all still missing. Whatever your role, treat these products as outside clinical care, and write down exactly what you were told.

Do not prescribe, supply, supervise or recommend a research-use-only product, and do not read its certificate as permission. Record the product, lot and supplier the patient names, and your advice to stop.
If a patient brings a research-use-only vial or its certificate, record the product name, lot and supplier exactly as printed, do not handle or administer it, and tell the prescriber the same day.
You can explain what a certificate does and does not show. You cannot vouch for a research product, and anyone injecting one should see a prescriber.

In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where it could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)). The Directive's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).

In Portugal, a medicine is any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings to make a medical diagnosis or to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento). Making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisations or registrations is an administrative offence punishable by a fine from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or food supplement) and so are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use. ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used only in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 has, since 2 January 2025, barred importing, distributing, possessing, selling, displaying or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans, or for therapeutic purposes outside an approved study or clinical trial, and bars facilities from buying peptide products from websites, social media or unverifiable suppliers (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) prohibits compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, unless the DoH permits it.

Regulatory status (outside the US)
Selling and advertising peptides outside the US.

Outside the US, whether a peptide is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, not on the category a seller chooses, and a medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's prior approval.
Medicine or not: what is claimed, and what it is and does
No marketing authorisation: no sale, supply or advertising
Prescription-only: public advertising banned or approved first
Is it a medicine?
Regulators look at what is claimed for a product and at what it is and does. A research-use label or a cosmetic box does not settle it.
Without authorisation
A medicine with no marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised, whatever the label calls it.
Prescription-only

Selling a peptide outside the United States starts with one question, whether the product is a medicine, and regulators answer it from the product itself. They look at what is claimed for it and at what it is and does, so a research-use label or a cosmetic box settles nothing. A medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's approval first, and that covers posts on social media by clinics and influencers. The details differ from country to country, so check the rules for your own jurisdiction, shown with this moment, and date what you find.

In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims, including websites and social media, and from its form and the way it is used. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. MHRA classes injectable melanotan products as medicines, and its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. Prescription-only medicines may not be advertised to the public at all: a clinic may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the medicine, and in February 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled that influencer posts tagging a weight-loss injection were adverts for a prescription-only medicine. GMC guidance requires doctors to examine a patient physically before prescribing an injectable cosmetic medicine.

In the EU, member states must prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and any advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public, where advertising includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 86 to 88). EU audiovisual law also bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU).

In Portugal, advertising a medicine without a valid national authorisation or registration, or one authorised under Articles 92 and 93, is prohibited, prescription-only medicines may be advertised only in technical media for health professionals, and the advertiser, the agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the medium are all liable (Estatuto do Medicamento). Health advertising practices fall under Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects and is enforced by the Health Regulatory Authority (ERS).

In Brazil, advertising of prescription-only medicines on the internet must be accessible exclusively to professionals authorised to prescribe or dispense them, through an electronic registration system (RDC 96/2008), and ANVISA restated in November 2024 that advertising compounded products to the public is not permitted. Lesson 7.3 · Concept
Off-label needs a label.

Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug for a use its labelling does not cover, and FDA accepts it as clinical judgment. A never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, so prescribing it is use of an unapproved drug. Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA's 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy named BPC-157 and GHK-Cu on exactly this basis.
Off-label applies only to approved drugs
A never-approved peptide has no label
Compounded is still unapproved
Off-label
An approved drug, used outside its labelling. FDA accepts this as the prescriber's judgment when it is medically appropriate.
Unapproved
A peptide that was never approved has no labelling to depart from. The Peptide Pocket Guide names prescribing it for what it is, use of an unapproved drug.
Compounded
A 503A or 503B product is also unapproved. It is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions.

Off-label is the phrase to get right first. FDA uses it for an approved drug prescribed outside its labelling, which prescribers generally may do when they judge it medically appropriate. The idea assumes a label exists. A peptide that was never approved has none, so prescribing it counts as using an unapproved drug, and the Peptide Pocket Guide says exactly that. Compounding leaves that answer unchanged. A compounded product is unapproved by definition, and it is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions. Under federal law, putting an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act, and in 2020 FDA warned a compounding pharmacy about its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products on that basis. So write the real category in the chart, every time.

In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)). A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise (Estatuto do Medicamento), and INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians keep the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks, while no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu that promise aesthetic effects or improvement in health conditions are not registered with ANVISA, and that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 lets a physician prescribe a medical product for a use not in its leaflet, or one never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH allows peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026).
