Same molecule, different rulebooks.
Route and claim decide the regime, whatever the molecule. Here is how each one treats a skin peptide in the US, as checked in September 2026.
Cosmetic
Appearance claims only
No premarket approval. A claim to affect structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', makes it a drug; 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
Dietary supplement
Oral, no disease claims
The maker is responsible for safety and labelling before sale; FDA acts after products reach the market.
Approved drug
Labelled indications
Off-label use of an approved drug is lawful clinical judgment; document the reasoning.
Compounded (503A or 503B)
Unapproved, conditionally lawful
Only when the substance qualifies and the pharmacy meets the statute. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is in Category 1; BPC-157 and TB-500 have no route.
Investigational or research use only
Trials, or nothing
Human use belongs in a clinical trial. A 'research use only' vial is outside any clinical route.
Write the regime in the chart in these words, before anything else.
The UK sorts products the same way, by claim, form and use, into cosmetics, food and medicines; lesson 7.2 set out its route for unlicensed medicines.

In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)); anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)). Food supplements are foods, and a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims (Directive 2002/46/EC; Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics and states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not cosmetics (read 25 September 2026). Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease, and must be notified to DGAV before sale; DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12), and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist and that, if a product is offered in this form, it is an irregular cosmetic. A food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion by healthy people (RDC 243/2018), and it may use only constituents on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018).

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 makes cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and food supplements, medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023), while ordinary cosmetics need a MoIAT conformity certificate (Cabinet Resolution 18/2014); an EDE classification letter settles whether a product needs EDE marketing authorisation and in which regulatory category. In Abu Dhabi, the DoH keeps topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect on existing pathways as low-risk products, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (31 July 2026).

What do you tell her?
Agree to supervise once she signs a consent form.
Research use only is not a clinical pathway. Do not prescribe, supply, supervise or recommend a research-use-only product.
Decline to supervise, supply or recommend it: a research-use-only product stays outside clinical care.
Right. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the 'not for use in humans' disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions.
Agree to supervise if the certificate shows high purity.

She asks whether a 503A compounding pharmacy could make GHK-Cu injections for her instead. In the US, what does FDA's record show, as checked in September 2026?
GHK-Cu is in Category 1, so a 503A pharmacy can compound it for injection.

Right. FDA's safety concerns stay posted, and withdrawal is not clearance. Check the live list on the day: GHK-Cu alone moved twice in April and May 2026.
It could be prescribed as off-label use.

'Off-label GHK-Cu; patient advised.'

The product, lot and supplier she names, its status in plain words, your advice to stop, her decision and the date you checked FDA's lists.
Right. Record the product, lot and supplier the patient names and your advice to stop, and date the status check: FDA's lists changed in April and May 2026.
Nothing, because you prescribed nothing.

Final check · Hormones and Peptides for Skin
A single-cell RNA atlas predicts that a skin cell type can make a hormone. What would move that finding toward proof of secretion?
Showing the hormone protein and its release by those cells, then its effect in tissue or in people.
Correct. RNA is the first rung; protein, release and function are the next.
Finding the same RNA in a second atlas.
Replicating the RNA confirms the transcript, which is still a prediction about secretion.
Finding the hormone's receptor RNA in neighbouring cells.
That predicts a possible receiver; it does not show the hormone is made or released.
Transcriptomic maps predict capacity; secretion and function need protein-level and functional evidence, and clinical use needs human trials.
Which finding is a local cutaneous feedback loop rather than systemic endocrine signalling?
Skin-made vitamin D3 carried by the blood to the liver.
That is the skin supplying a whole-body hormone system: skin to body.
Human scalp follicles in culture secrete cortisol and then reduce their own CRH.
Correct. Made, sensed and fed back within the follicle, with no systemic connection.
Thin skin and striae in Cushing syndrome.
Circulating cortisol excess acting on the skin: body to skin.
A local loop is made and used within the skin; systemic signals travel through the blood, in either direction.
Why can a blood or saliva cortisol level not tell you how much cortisol a patient's skin is generating?
Because 11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells, and local availability is regulated independently of circulating levels.
Correct: a mechanism shown in human skin samples and mice.
Because skin cells cannot make or activate cortisol.
They can: skin expresses an HPA-like axis, and 11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol locally.
Because saliva and blood cortisol tests are unreliable for everything.
Late-night salivary cortisol is a first-line test for Cushing's syndrome; it measures systemic cortisol, which is a different question.
Local tissue cortisol and systemic cortisol are separate: the first is a research mechanism, the second is what diagnostic tests measure.
A patient asks whether starting hormone therapy at menopause will stop her wrinkles. Which answer fits the evidence?
Yes: estrogen rebuilds collagen, so her wrinkles will improve.
Small trials show thicker skin, but the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles.
It may thicken the skin a little, the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles, and skin is not a reason to start; hot flashes or vaginal symptoms are worth discussing with a prescriber.
Correct: a secondary effect, and an indication-led decision.
It has no effect on skin at all.
Small RCTs do show gains in thickness and collagen; what is unproven is a visible wrinkle benefit.
Separate structural effects (small trials) from visible ageing (large trials) and from indications (symptoms and bone).
A colleague says tirzepatide is 'GRADE A', so its effect on the face must be well established. What is wrong with that reasoning?
Nothing: a drug's grade applies to all of its effects.
Grades attach to a specific outcome in a specific population. The pivotal trials measured weight and never the face.
Grades attach to outcomes: weight loss is A from large randomized trials, while facial change rests on small observational studies.
Correct. One grade per outcome.
Tirzepatide has no GRADE A evidence for anything.
It does, for weight management and type 2 diabetes, from large randomized trials such as SURMOUNT-1.

An evidence grade belongs to a statement, not to a molecule. SURMOUNT-1 supports an A for weight loss; facial change rests on a 20-patient imaging study and a patient survey (C to D), and no randomized trial has measured the face.
Which statement about the gut–skin link is best supported by the evidence?
Probiotic capsules reliably clear eczema by repairing the gut barrier.
Pooled trials show little or no difference in patient-rated eczema symptoms.
Metabolic endotoxaemia is shown in mice and small human studies, but restoring the gut barrier has not been shown to improve disease outside the gut.
Correct. Mechanism in mice and short-term human physiology; no proof that barrier repair helps the skin.
A zonulin blood test identifies patients whose skin disease comes from a leaky gut.
A widely used zonulin assay detects proteins other than zonulin.

High-fat feeding raises circulating endotoxin in mice and briefly in healthy men; a leading review finds it unproven that restoring barrier function improves disease outside the gut, and Cochrane found little or no patient-rated benefit from probiotics in eczema.
Which statement about topical GHK-Cu keeps its evidence and its regulatory status apart correctly?
It is GRADE C on small trials, and in the US its non-injectable form sits in 503A Category 1, which means under evaluation.
Correct. Two separate answers: small-trial human evidence, and an enforcement posture that is not an approval.
Its Category 1 listing shows FDA has found it effective for skin.
Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating; it says nothing about efficacy.
Its copper-enzyme mechanism makes its evidence grade A.
A plausible mechanism is not human evidence; the trials are small (C).
Mechanism, human evidence and regulatory status are separate registers; GHK-Cu scores differently on each.
Oral collagen trials pooled together look positive. What did splitting them by funding and quality show?
The benefit held in every subgroup.
It did not: independent and high-quality trials showed no effect.
The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and lower-quality trials.
Correct — Myung and Park, 2025, 23 RCTs.
Independent trials showed harm.
No harm signal was reported; the finding is about absence of benefit.
Funding and study quality can explain a pooled effect; ask who ran the trial before what it showed.
Which statement about afamelanotide and Melanotan II is accurate?
Afamelanotide is approved (EU 2014, US 2019) only for erythropoietic protoporphyria; Melanotan II is approved for no indication, and regulators in the US, UK and Australia have warned about it.
Correct. Same receptor family, different molecules, and only one has an approval, for one rare disease.
Afamelanotide's US approval covers cosmetic tanning.
The US indication is to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with EPP; tanning is not an approved use.
Melanotan II became approvable once FDA reviewed it for compounding.
Its compounding nomination was withdrawn, and FDA's page lists serious safety risks. A review is never an approval.
Approval attaches to a specific product and indication; a shared receptor transfers neither evidence nor legal standing.
A patient asks about a PTD-DBM hair spray. Which grade fits its evidence, and why?
A, because it acts on the central Wnt pathway of hair growth.
A plausible pathway is mechanism, and grades rest on human evidence.
D: one 2017 study in mice and scalp tissue from the developer's group, and no human trial published or registered as of September 2026.
Correct. Animal and tissue data only, from one group with a commercial link.
C, because small human trials show regrowth.
No human trial of PTD-DBM exists, small or large.
Grade the human evidence, then say who produced it; a strong mechanism with no trial in people is D.
In the US, as of September 2026, which statement about growth-hormone secretagogues and 503A compounding is accurate?
Ipamorelin and CJC-1295 are on the 503A bulks list, because clinics compound them widely.
Neither is on the list. FDA's advisory committee voted against ipamorelin in 2024, and both 503A nominations were withdrawn.
None of them is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren is in FDA's Category 2 for a heart-failure signal, and the ipamorelin and CJC-1295 nominations were withdrawn.
Correct, dated to FDA's category documents of April and May 2026.
Sermorelin is an FDA-approved product marketed for adult anti-ageing.
No sermorelin product is marketed in the US. Its former approvals were for children with GH deficiency and for diagnostic testing.
Popularity and compounding volume are not regulatory standing; check the live FDA lists and name the date.
Why does a 'low' IGF-1 in a healthy 60-year-old not, on its own, justify growth-hormone therapy?
IGF-1 falls normally with age, and trials in healthy older adults show small body-composition gains with more oedema, joint pain and glucose problems.
Correct. The somatopause is physiology, and the trials point against treatment.
Because growth hormone has no effect on skin at all.
GH acts on dermal fibroblasts, and GH excess visibly changes skin. The problem is the balance of benefit and harm in healthy adults.
Because IGF-1 cannot be measured reliably.
IGF-1 is a standard test. The point is to read it against an age-matched range and to treat a diagnosis.
Treat confirmed deficiency, not ageing: age-adjusted ranges plus the healthy-ageing trials.
In GRADE, what does a certainty rating attach to?
A single well-run trial.
GRADE rates a body of evidence, never one study on its own.
The molecule, across all its uses.
The same molecule can be high certainty for one outcome and very low for another.
A body of evidence for a specific outcome.
Correct. Certainty belongs to an outcome, across the studies that address it.
Name the outcome before you name the grade; risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias can each lower it.
Under section 503A, in what order does the statute let a bulk substance qualify for compounding?
The bulks list first, then a monograph, then a component of an approved drug.
Reversed. The bulks list is the last route, open only when the first two are not.
A USP or NF monograph first, then a component of an approved drug, then the 503A bulks list, with a valid certificate of analysis in every case.
Correct. The routes are hierarchical, and the certificate and a registered manufacturer are conditions throughout.
Any substance whose certificate of analysis shows high purity.
A certificate is a condition, never a route on its own.
The statute's routes are hierarchical, and as of September 2026 no peptide sits on the six-substance bulks list.

The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues and predicted which cell types could make or respond to hormones. Its own authors call these predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA shows capacity, not secretion or effect. Treat any 'skin has receptors for it' product claim as a hypothesis until protein, function and a human trial back it. A few skin outputs are established in people, such as vitamin D3 formed under UVB and released into the blood.
A product says skin has receptors for it. Does that prove it works?

Senescent cells accumulate in human epidermis and dermis with age, and in one cohort their number tracked with wrinkles and perceived age: an association. Their secretions (the SASP: IL-6, IL-8, matrix-degrading enzymes) were defined in cultured cells. Evidence that clearing senescent cells improves ageing comes from mice; human data are small open-label or exploratory pilots measuring tissue markers. The one randomized study in skin (topical rapamycin, a senomorphic, 2019) was small and exploratory: it lowered p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026). In mice, clearing senescent cells during healing slowed wound closure. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises confining senolytics to clinical trials. This course gives no doses or product advice; daily sunscreen and topical retinoids are the levers with human trials, and a prescriber decides on any treatment.
Do senolytics help ageing skin?

Most 'cortisol face' is puffiness from sleep, alcohol, salt and weight, as the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide describes it. Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is rare (two to three new cases per million people a year), and its commonest form comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is using, so ask about tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-lighteners. The features that best discriminate Cushing's are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness and reddish-purple striae wider than 1 cm; a round face alone is a weak signal. If several are present and progressing, the next step is formal testing arranged by a prescriber and an endocrinologist, not a supplement or a consumer cortisol panel. Local skin cortisol (11β-HSD1) is a research mechanism with no approved treatment.
When is a “cortisol face” a sign of Cushing's syndrome?

Estrogen acts on receptors in skin. In small trials, hormone therapy thickened skin and raised collagen (graded C here). The largest trial on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks) and a four-year trial in recently menopausal women found no difference in wrinkles. In the US, as of February 2026, approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss; skin is not an indication and is never the reason to start. Compounded 'bioidentical' hormones lack efficacy and safety data, and an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug under US rules. In the UK, HRT products are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis; skin is not among their uses, and a compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine that MHRA guidance places behind any licensed product that meets the need. For skin, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid have better evidence. This course gives no doses; hormone therapy decisions belong with a prescriber.
Does HRT help wrinkles?

'Ozempic face' describes facial hollowing and laxity during weight loss on incretin drugs. Mechanism: losing fat deflates the superficial facial fat compartments and unmasks laxity already present. Human evidence is observational and small: one retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial, about 7% per 10 kg lost (D), and a survey of 1,226 patients found sagging, facial volume loss and hair shedding reported more often the more weight was lost (C). No randomized trial has measured the face. Regulatory status (US, September 2026): semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) are FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, chronic weight management and further heart, liver and sleep-apnoea indications. Their labels list hair loss (about 3–6% on drug against about 1% on placebo, mostly in women, linked to weight reduction) but not facial volume loss. In the UK (September 2026), Ozempic is licensed for type 2 diabetes, Wegovy for weight management and cardiovascular risk reduction, and Mounjaro for both type 2 diabetes and weight management; UK product information also lists hair loss, and MHRA says retatrutide is not authorised in the UK. Open question: whether the drugs act directly on facial fat, beyond weight loss, rests on cell studies. In practice: raise facial and hair changes before treatment, record concerns with consented photographs, refer restoration requests to a qualified aesthetic clinician, and take any question about stopping or changing the medicine to the prescriber. The course gives no dosing advice.
What causes “Ozempic face”?

Mechanism: bacterial lipopolysaccharide crossing a leaky gut barrier ('metabolic endotoxaemia') drives inflammation and insulin resistance in mice, and a single high-fat meal briefly raised plasma endotoxin in a study of 12 healthy men (D). Human evidence for skin: an independent Cochrane review of 39 trials found probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated eczema symptoms (B); a 2024 meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported small score improvements (C); one small randomized trial found rosacea improved after small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth was treated (C). A leading review concludes it is unproven that restoring barrier function improves disease outside the gut, and a widely used commercial zonulin assay detects proteins other than zonulin. A fibre-rich diet has strong evidence for cardiometabolic outcomes and has not been tested on skin outcomes. The Hormonaly guide grades the 'leaky gut' repair stack (L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, BPC-157) D; in the US, BPC-157 is not on the 503A bulks list as of September 2026. In the UK, an unlicensed medicine can be supplied as a 'special' only for an individual patient's special clinical need that no licensed product meets, on the prescriber's responsibility. Start with diet, metabolic health and the skin diagnosis; investigational peptides come last, if at all, and any injected or research peptide needs a prescriber.
Does a leaky gut cause skin problems?

Topical GHK-Cu has a plausible copper-enzyme mechanism and small-trial human support (GRADE C); injected GHK-Cu has no randomized trials and commonly irritates. In the US, as of FDA's 14 May 2026 list, non-injectable GHK-Cu is in 503A Category 1 (under evaluation, not approved); the injectable route is excluded. In the UK, a GHK-Cu serum presented for appearance is regulated as a cosmetic, and cosmetics law excludes anything injected; MHRA decides from its claims, form and use whether an injected product is a medicine, and a medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice — for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.
What does the evidence show for copper peptides (GHK-Cu)?

BPC-157's evidence is rodent studies from one group plus uncontrolled case series; no randomized efficacy trial in people has been published in full (September 2026); the one randomized trial FDA found, in ulcerative colitis, exists only as a 2005 meeting abstract and showed no significant difference from placebo. TB-500 is a seven-residue fragment of thymosin beta-4 that has never been trialled; KPV has only mouse data. GLOW and KLOW are marketing names for untested blends. FDA's advisory committee reviewed BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 in July 2026 — advice only; they are not on the 503A bulks list. In the UK, a medicine with no marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and MHRA's largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. New pigmentation while using research-use-only peptides is a red flag: stop, record the product and source, and get it assessed.
Is there human evidence for BPC-157?

Afamelanotide (Scenesse) is an MC1R agonist approved only for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EU 2014, US 2019; licensed in the UK, where NICE did not recommend it for NHS use in 2023), on the strength of two sponsor-funded phase 3 trials; even there, the US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice a year. Melanotan II is a different, non-selective molecule approved for no indication. Its only controlled human data are two tiny 1990s studies, and case reports describe darkening and new moles, nail pigmentation, melanomas in people with other risk factors (causation unproven), priapism and rhabdomyolysis. FDA (April 2026), MHRA (April 2024) and TGA (August 2026) have all put warnings on record. If someone has used it: stop, record the product and seller, examine the skin and nails, and refer changing moles; a personal or family history of melanoma makes it an absolute no in the endocrinology guide. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.
What are the risks of a tanning injection such as Melanotan II?

PTD-DBM releases a brake (CXXC5) on Wnt signalling; its whole evidence is one 2017 mouse and tissue study from the developer's group, with no human trial published or registered as of September 2026 (grade D). Zinc thymulin is a zinc-dependent thymic peptide with no indexed human hair study (grade D). In the US, on FDA's 14 May 2026 lists, thymulin acetate is in 503A Category 3 and PTD-DBM is on no list; neither is on the bulks list. Hair loss starts with a workup (pattern, trigger, patches, androgens; ferritin and TSH in everyone), and the approved options, minoxidil, finasteride in men and baricitinib for severe alopecia areata, carry grade A evidence. In the UK, a men's minoxidil foam is on general sale, finasteride for hair loss is a private prescription carrying MHRA's strengthened warnings on depression and sexual dysfunction (May 2026), baricitinib is licensed for severe alopecia areata, and a peptide spray made up for one patient would be an unlicensed special that MHRA guidance places behind any licensed product that could meet the need. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; treatment choices belong with the prescriber.
Is there a peptide for hair loss with human trials?

Tesamorelin is the one peptide on this axis with approval-grade evidence: two phase 3 trials and US approval (2010) for excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy, GRADE A for that use only. Sermorelin, CJC-1295 with DAC and ipamorelin have human hormone-level data but no trial showing a clinical or skin benefit; CJC-1295 without DAC and IGF-1 LR3 have no published human studies (this course grades all of these D). In the US, as of FDA's lists of April and May 2026, no growth-hormone secretagogue is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren (MK-677) is in Category 2, and the CJC-1295 and ipamorelin 503A nominations were withdrawn. Growth hormone itself is approved for diagnosed deficiency and a few growth disorders, and knowingly distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence in the US. In the UK, somatropin is a prescription-only medicine and a Class C controlled drug, and MHRA's products database holds no product information for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin (September 2026). This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; for an individual patient, that is a prescriber's decision.
What do growth hormone peptides do for skin?

Signs of growth-hormone excess include puffy, thickened skin of the face, hands and feet, oily skin, more sweating, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, tight rings or shoes, night-time tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention with swelling and joint pain is common and usually settles when treatment stops. The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 testing when typical acral and facial features are present, so route these patients to a prescriber or to endocrinology. On cancer, keep four answers apart: the IGF-1 receptor drives cell growth (mechanism); higher natural IGF-1 goes with modestly higher risk of some cancers (observation); GH replacement in true deficiency has not shown a clear risk in large cohorts; and for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for skin, long-term cancer data do not exist (open question).
What are the signs of too much growth hormone?

GRADE rates certainty for a specific outcome across a body of evidence: high, moderate, low or very low (the Hormonaly guides print A to D). Randomized trials start high; certainty drops for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias. Industry-sponsored studies more often report favourable results (Cochrane, 2017), so ask who ran and paid for the trials. A grade is separate from legal status: check both, and never let a mechanism raise a grade. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.
How good is the evidence behind a “clinically proven” claim?

In the US, a 503A pharmacy may compound only from a substance that meets a USP or NF monograph, or else is a component of an approved drug, or else is on the 503A bulks list (six substances, none a peptide, as of September 2026), and it needs a valid certificate of analysis. A certificate is the supplier's report on one lot: mass spectrometry for identity, HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin and microbial results. It cannot prove your vial is that lot, how it was stored, or that it is sterile or lawful. 'Research use only' products are labelled not for use in humans, and 'off-label' applies only to approved drugs. In the UK, an unlicensed medicine reaches a patient as a 'special', made by a licensed specials manufacturer to a prescriber's order for one patient's special clinical need, or as a medicine a pharmacist prepares against a prescription; MHRA guidance ranks a UK-licensed medicine, even used off-label, ahead of an unlicensed one, and specials may not be advertised. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.
What does a certificate of analysis (COA) prove about purity?

reviewJobs.sourceText: Hormones and Peptides for Skin

Designed toward future CME accreditation, this post-graduate clinical course prepares aesthetic and dermatologic clinicians to appraise the endocrine physiology of skin, differentiate pathognomonic endocrine cutaneous signs from isolated cosmetic presentations, evaluate the GRADE evidence and pharmacodynamics of cutaneous peptides and incretin therapies, and navigate regulatory and liability boundaries without promoting unapproved dosing protocols or commercial bias.

Continuing professional education for licensed clinicians and allied providers. Every learner gets the same evidence, regulatory status and safety content; what each may do with it — prescribe, recommend, administer, or refer — follows their own licence and scope, and the course adapts its practice guidance to that role. It informs clinical reasoning; it is not a protocol, contains no dosing, and does not replace specialist input, formal guidelines or individual judgment.
Educational content for clinicians. It does not prescribe, and it never restates an evidence grade above what the source assigns to the specific indication.

Regulatory statements name their jurisdiction and date. US status (FDA, 503A/503B compounding) is given in the lesson text; status in the United Kingdom, the European Union, Portugal, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates (federal, with Dubai and Abu Dhabi where they differ) is given in each moment's regulatory note, read from each regulator's own primary sources in September 2026, and the learner's own country is shown first. The US compounding categories have no equivalent in the other jurisdictions. Check the live status with the national regulator before acting.
Designed toward future CME accreditation. No CME or CE credit is currently offered.

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 1 — the four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) and the three routes (local, neural, circulation) · PMID 40263492 · Publisher correction PMID 40316721. Guide reference resolves exactly.

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 3, ch.6 ref 3, ch.7 ref 4 — CRH, POMC, ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin are made in skin with their receptors (para/autocrine action); dermal and epidermal units · PMID 11041445 · Erratum 2002. Also cited by A&RE ch.7 for the estrogen–senescence statement, which this 2000 review does not address (see findings).

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 4, ch.7 ref 2 — skin makes, activates and releases hormones, including sex steroids that matter for the whole organism, especially in older people · PMID 16982574 · Verified; no PMCID.
narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 13 — sensory nerves and neuropeptides as the neural arm of the skin's signalling network · PMID 17015491 · Verified.

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 4 — skin cells hold the full apparatus (CYP11A1 onward) to make glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens or activate circulating precursors; the review also describes a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens · PMID 23435015 · Verified.

mouse genetic model (keratinocyte Cyp11b1 deletion) plus human disease association · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 5 — keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation; the functional proof is in mice · PMID 33514551 · The guide presents this without naming the species; the course labels it as animal evidence.

human scalp hair follicles in organ culture (ex vivo) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 11 — CRH → POMC/ACTH → cortisol secretion with glucocorticoid feedback on CRH, in follicles with no systemic connections · PMID 15946990 · Verified.

research letter; human follicles ex vivo · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 12 — a GH/IGF-1 loop in the follicle · PMID 36496194 · No abstract indexed and not open access; cited only for the finding its title states.

narrative review (mouse models of thyroid-hormone metabolism) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 7 — local deiodinase control of T3 in keratinocytes; the review says the mechanisms are being clarified mainly in mouse models · PMID 33683663 · Verified.

human skin photobiology · academic · role: the skin-to-body example: previtamin D3 forms in human skin under solar UV and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation by vitamin D-binding protein · PMID 6251551 · Not cited by either guide; added as the primary for the statement that skin supplies a whole-body hormone system.
narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 3 — vitamin D3 made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol, then 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D elsewhere · PMID 24529992 · Verified.

clinical review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 8 — the skin signs of thyroid disease (myxoedema; dry, coarse skin) · PMID 22110782 · Verified (a 2012 review with the same title exists, PMID 22914563; the guide's volume and pages match this one).

single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas (hormone2cell): 379 hormone and receptor genes, ~14 million cells and nuclei, 47 human tissues · academic (University of Cambridge, Wellcome Sanger Institute) · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 1 — predicted hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types; the transcriptomic map the lesson is about · PMID 42207862 · PubMed entry 2026-05-28 (the guide's 'published online May 28, 2026'); print issue 2 Jul 2026. Full text and supplement paywalled (HTTP 403); only abstract- and portal-level facts are taught.

data portal · atlas authors · role: the authors' own usage statement: predictions are 'putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than … functional hormones and receptors', validation is the user's responsibility; 47 disease-free tissues, 1,900+ cell types, 14 million+ cells; skin is listed among the tissues on the sister cellxgene site (hormonecellatlas.cellgeni.sanger.ac.uk) · Fetched live 2026-09-24 (HTTP 200).

narrative review · academic · role: transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios · PMID 27104977 · Not cited by either guide; added to support the RNA-versus-protein step.

systematic review (MOOSE): 4 experimental studies, 3 field trials (2 RCTs), 69 observational studies · academic (QIMR Berghofer, Australian National University) · role: tests the guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use: experiments with artificial UV show a block; randomized field trials of daily sunscreen (SPF ~16) show no fall; high-SPF products untested · PMID 30945275 · Not cited by either guide; contradicts A&RE ch.7 testing pearl (see findings).

cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells after genotoxic stress (+ prostate tumours after chemotherapy) · academic · role: defines the SASP (IL-6, IL-8 and other secreted factors) — the concept the guide uses · PMID 19053174 · Not cited by either guide; the primary behind 'SASP'.

human skin tissue bank, cross-sectional (0–20, 21–70, 71–95 years) · academic · role: p16-positive cells are more numerous in older skin, in both epidermis and dermis · PMID 16911562 · Not cited by either guide.

cohort (Leiden Longevity Study), n=178, aged 45–81, sun-protected upper-inner-arm biopsies · academic; one co-author from Unilever; NIH and Cancer Research UK grants · role: senescent-cell counts in human skin track with elastic-fibre changes, facial wrinkles and perceived age, independent of chronological age; lowest vs highest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked ~3 years younger · PMID 26286607 · Not cited by either guide.
narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 5 — senescent cells accumulate in several human skin compartments; cell types respond differently · PMID 34166688 · Verified.

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 6 — no universal biomarker identifies senescent cells unequivocally; markers by skin compartment · PMID 30190724 · Full text (PMC6115505) read: it does not discuss estrogen loss or hormone responsiveness, which A&RE ch.7 cites it for.

narrative review (no new data) · three authors from L'Oréal and a senolytic-field investigator; declares no competing interests · role: how dermatologic senotherapy stands in 2026: a review of mechanism and prospects; transient senescence aids wound repair · PMID 42417965 · Not cited by either guide.

cross-sectional reference measurements of forearm skin · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 1 — skin collagen falls with age and is lower in women at all ages · PMID 1220811 · The abstract gives no annual rate; the guide's '~1% per year' could not be checked and is not taught.

human skin sections (18–29 vs 80+ years) and isolated dermal fibroblasts · academic · role: aged fibroblasts make less procollagen and are less attached to and stretched by collagen — two routes to lower synthesis · PMID 16723701 · Not cited by either guide.

aged (>80) vs young (21–30) human skin in vivo, plus organ and collagen-lattice culture · academic · role: more fibroblast MMP-1 in aged human dermis; fragmented collagen lowers fibroblast stretch and raises MMP-1 and oxidants — a self-perpetuating loop · PMID 19116368 · Not cited by either guide.

narrative review with new data · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 2 — UV drives the matrix breakdown of photoageing, and photoageing and chronological ageing share molecular pathways · PMID 12437452 · Verified.

mouse (INK-ATTAC transgene) · academic · role: A&RE ch.13 ref 2 — clearing p16-positive cells from one year of age extended median lifespan and delayed kidney, heart and fat deterioration; skin was checked for safety only (thickness, fibrosis), and clearance during healing slowed wound closure (Extended Data Fig. 10) · PMID 26840489 · Verified.

mouse, plus human adipose-tissue explants · several authors hold a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds senolytic patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 1 — senescent cells cause dysfunction when transplanted; senolytics improved function and post-treatment survival in old mice · PMID 29988130 · Verified.

open-label phase 1 pilot, n=9, diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131) · investigators with a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 3 — after a short course, epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells and circulating SASP factors fell; tissue-marker endpoints only · PMID 31542391 · Corrigendum PMID 31982828. The course does not report doses.

exploratory placebo-controlled RCT; 36 enrolled, 19 discontinued or lost to follow-up (NCT03103893) · academic (Drexel University) · role: the one randomized study of a senomorphic in human skin found: p16 protein fell and collagen VII rose; clinical change described only in 'multiple participants' · PMID 31761958 · Not cited by either guide.

community RCT (Nambour), n=903 adults under 55, 4.5 years, blinded assessors (ACTRN12610000086066) · public (National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia) · role: daily sunscreen: no detectable increase in skin ageing over 4.5 years and 24% less ageing than discretionary use · PMID 23732711 · Not cited by either guide (A&RE ch.10 recommends sun protection without a trial citation).

systematic review of 7 RCTs · academic; no conflicts declared · role: the randomized-trial base behind the guide's GRADE A for topical retinoids in photoageing: consistent improvement in wrinkling, mottled pigmentation and lentigines · PMID 35620028 · A&RE gives no citation for its GRADE A; this review supplies one.

randomized double-blind vehicle-controlled arm comparison, n=36, mean age 87, 24 weeks · academic (NIH-supported) · role: retinol improved fine wrinkling of naturally aged skin; biopsy subgroups showed more glycosaminoglycan and procollagen I · PMID 17515510 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

human sun-protected skin by age group (n=72) plus one-week topical retinol in 53 people aged 80+ · academic · role: aged skin shows more MMPs and less collagen synthesis; one week of topical retinol lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis · PMID 10692106 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

human skin explants and primary dermal fibroblasts; mouse skin · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts express 11β-HSD1 (not 11β-HSD2); activity rises with donor age; photo-exposed fibroblasts express more; glucocorticoid availability is regulated at a pre-receptor level, independently of systemic levels · PMID 20739946 · A&RE ch.8 ref 2; verified

human skin biopsies (young vs older; photo-exposed vs photo-protected) + 11β-HSD1 knockout mice · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: 11β-HSD1 activity elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin; knockout mice protected from age-induced dermal atrophy; physiological cortisol inhibits collagen biosynthesis in dermal fibroblasts · PMID 23722901 · not cited by the guides; open access PMC3696573

investigator-initiated double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b pilot, n=28 adults with type 2 diabetes, 35 days · academic lead (University of Leeds); AstraZeneca co-authors · role: the only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes: primary outcome (ex vivo skin 11β-HSD1 activity) not met; exploratory smaller wound diameter; improved epidermal integrity but modestly impaired barrier function · PMID 35113805 · not cited by the guides; registered NCT03313297; the drug regimen is deliberately not reproduced (the lock excludes dosing)

registered phase 2 pilot · academic · role: status: the only registered trial of an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor with skin outcomes found (ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, 2026-09-24, terms '11beta-HSD1', '11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 inhibitor', AZD4017, SPI-62, clofutriben); none tests skin ageing. AZD4017 has no Drugs@FDA record (openFDA drugsfda query, 2026-09-24) · CT.gov API 2026-09-24; results published as Ajjan 2022

clinical practice guideline (GRADE) · professional society (Endocrine Society) · role: A&RE ch.8 ref 5. Table 1: features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome = easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, striae (especially reddish-purple and >1 cm wide); common and/or less discriminatory = facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, supraclavicular fullness, weight gain, obesity, acne, hirsutism, thin skin, fatigue, insomnia. 3.1 drug history first (oral, rectal, inhaled, topical, injected; skin creams incl. bleaching agents, herbal tonics, joint or nerve injections). 3.2 test multiple and progressive features or features unusual for age. 3.3 against widespread testing. 3.5 against random serum cortisol. Abnormal result → endocrinologist. Endogenous incidence 2–3 per million per year (European population studies); commonest cause iatrogenic. · PMID 18334580 · full text read at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC2386281) 2026-09-24; test names only, doses not reproduced

narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.9 ref 2 and the single reference NAMS 2022 cites for its skin key point; quotes collagen falling 'by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause' citing Brincat 1985 and Affinito 1999 · PMID 24194966 · open access PMC3772914, read in full 2026-09-24

vehicle-controlled in vivo biopsy study, n=70 (40 postmenopausal women, 30 men, mean age 75), 2 weeks · academic (University of Michigan) · role: ERα, ERβ and GPR30 expressed similarly in aged and photoaged skin; topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III and collagen I in sun-protected hip skin but not in photoaged forearm or face · PMID 18794456 · registered NCT00113100; concentrations deliberately not reproduced

biopsy comparison of implant-treated vs untreated postmenopausal women · academic (London) · role: in untreated women skin collagen declined in relation to years since menopause, not chronological age · PMID 3978054 · cited by Thornton 2013 for the 30% figure; the abstract does not state it

observational study of postmenopausal women · academic (London) · role: skin collagen content, skin thickness and bone mass each declined by 1–2% per year after menopause, related to years since menopause · PMID 3120067 · primary source for the per-year figure

biopsy study, n=32 (14 pre-, 18 postmenopausal) · academic (Naples) · role: type I and III collagen lower after menopause; inversely correlated with years since menopause (and with age) · PMID 10656502 · cited by Thornton 2013 for the 30% figure; the abstract does not state it

double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=60, 12 months · academic (Québec); sponsor not stated in abstract · role: systemic conjugated estrogens increased skin thickness (biopsy, great-trochanter skin) vs placebo · PMID 8116726 · not cited by the guides; cited by Thornton 2013

double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=41, 6 months · academic (São Paulo) · role: upper-arm skin collagen rose 6.49% with HT only; other skin parameters unchanged · PMID 10687834 · not cited by the guides; regimen deliberately not reproduced

Module 01 · Opening film
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling.

Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.

Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Four units
Epidermis, dermis, subcutis and the adnexa each hold cells that make hormones and cells that react to them, from keratinocytes and fibroblasts to fat cells and mast cells.
Three routes
Signals pass between neighbouring cells, along sensory nerves, and into the blood, where they can reach distant organs.
What kind of evidence
The framework is drawn from cell, tissue and animal work. It explains how skin behaves; each finding in this module is labelled by the evidence behind it.

Mechanism
A steroid factory with local axes.

Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.

Local or systemic
Three directions of traffic.

Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.

Which direction?
One finding at a time: which way does the signal run?
Local loop
Body to skin
Skin to body
Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin
Local loop. Made and used where it is produced; the functional proof comes from mice that cannot make it in keratinocytes and develop skin inflammation.
UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to the liver
Skin to body. Vitamin D3 made in the skin is released into the circulation and activated elsewhere. Established human physiology.
Violaceous striae, thin skin and easy bruising in Cushing syndrome
Body to skin. Systemic cortisol excess acting on the dermis. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome as a reason to refer promptly.
Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol, then switch off their own CRH
Local loop, with its own feedback, running with no blood supply or nerves attached. Human tissue, ex vivo.
Skin converts circulating precursors into androgens and estrogens that add to the body's supply
Skin to body. Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids, more so in older people; the evidence is mainly biochemical.
Dry, coarse skin and myxoedema in hypothyroidism
Body to skin. Circulating thyroid hormone sets epidermal turnover and dermal matrix; the skin signs track the systemic deficit.
Scalp follicles convert testosterone to DHT, which shrinks susceptible follicles
Local loop. 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit makes DHT where it acts; the guide names it the substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia and hirsutism.
Seven placed. Three local loops, two signals the skin sends out, and two it receives.

What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.

The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment
The exam as a screen
Thinning and bruising, coarse dry skin, new acanthosis nigricans: each points to a systemic axis before it points to a serum.
When to refer
The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly.
Where local biology fits
Local loops explain how skin behaves day to day. The guide calls them foundation, never a reason to dose anyone with a hormone.

Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.
When a skin pattern suggests a systemic disorder, assess or refer before any cosmetic plan, and record that you considered it. Local skin biology is no basis for prescribing a hormone for appearance.
If you see new striae, rapid bruising, sudden hair change or signs of virilisation, record them and raise them with the prescriber before the next treatment.
If a client's skin change comes with new systemic symptoms, suggest they see a prescriber before trying another product. A serum cannot answer a systemic question.

Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.

The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
What it measured
RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes, cell by cell, across 47 human tissues including skin.
What it predicted
Which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond, including unexpected sites outside the classic glands.
What it leaves open
Whether a cell actually makes and releases the hormone, and whether that hormone does anything there.

Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.
A grid of small tissue tiles with a skin tile at the centre, where some cells carry receptor cups and a few hold outlined granules, marking cells predicted to respond to or make a hormone.
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.

The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.

Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D
Claims built on receptors
Receptors explain how a topical could act. Whether it does is a question for a human trial.
Local enzymes
Steroid-metabolising enzymes in skin change potency, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts.
Sunscreen and vitamin D
Artificial-UV experiments show sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis; field trials of daily use did not lower blood levels. High-protection products have not been trialled.

Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.

When a product or protocol is justified by 'skin has receptors for it', ask for the human trial before you prescribe. Assess vitamin D on clinical grounds, and do not advise patients to drop sun protection.
If a patient says they stopped sunscreen to raise their vitamin D, note it and pass it to the prescriber; the trials do not support stopping.
Describe receptor-based product claims as hypotheses unless a human trial backs them, keep sun-protection advice unchanged, and send vitamin D questions to a prescriber.

Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.

A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
A safety mechanism
A damaged cell stops dividing for good, which guards against cancer and helps wound repair.
The secretory phase
It stays active and releases inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors, first catalogued in cultured human cells.
What we see in human skin
Older skin holds more cells carrying the marker p16 in epidermis and dermis. No single marker is definitive.

Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.
On the left a cell divides into two; on the right a larger, flattened cell has stopped dividing and releases a cloud of small particles into the frayed fibres around it.

Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.

In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age
Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies
Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
Mechanism
A collagen-fragmentation loop

Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
Human evidence
Association
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Animal evidence
Causation, in mice
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.
Open question
Do senotherapies change human skin?

Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exploratory randomized trial of topical rapamycin (36 enrolled, 19 dropped out) lowered skin p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026).
A mouse lifespan result is not a skin treatment.
Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.

Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet
Sun protection
A publicly funded Australian trial of 903 adults: daily sunscreen meant about a quarter less skin ageing over four and a half years.
Retinoids
Consistent randomized trials for tretinoin in photoaged skin; the guide's GRADE A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in very old skin.
Senotherapies
Biomarker pilots only, so far. They sit below the levers that already have outcome data.

Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.

Module 02 · Opening film
Systemic hormones and the skin

Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist. Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the receptors to respond to them. They also carry an enzyme called eleven beta HSD one, which turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples that enzyme works harder with age and in sun-exposed skin, and it sets local cortisol independently of the level in the blood. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice bred without the enzyme kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Hold all of this in the mechanism register. It comes from biopsies, cultured cells and mice, and it says nothing yet about how a patient's face will age.
Mechanism
The skin regenerates its own cortisol.

Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.
Local axis: CRH, POMC and ACTH are made in skin
11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells
Mechanism register: human samples, cultured cells and mice
A local stress axis
Skin makes CRH and POMC-derived ACTH and carries their receptors, a field-restricted copy of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis.
Cortisol, regenerated
11β-HSD1 converts cortisone to cortisol in keratinocytes and fibroblasts. In human skin samples its activity rises with age and with sun exposure.
Why it matters for ageing
Cortisol slows collagen synthesis in fibroblasts, and knockout mice kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Whether this drives visible ageing in people has not been tested.

Discriminating or common?
Tap where each feature belongs.
Best discriminates Cushing's
Common, less discriminating
Easy bruising
One of the four features the guideline lists as best discriminating, particularly bruising with no obvious trauma.
Facial plethora
Listed among the best discriminators. Most of the four have low sensitivity, so their absence does not exclude the syndrome.
Proximal muscle weakness
Proximal myopathy is one of the four; ask about stairs and getting up from a low chair.
Striae
The guideline singles out striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm.
Facial fullness
The guideline lists facial fullness, like the dorsocervical fat pad, among features that are common in the general population. A round face alone is a weak signal.
Weight gain
Common and less discriminatory on its own; many features of cortisol excess are shared with ordinary obesity.
Acne or hirsutism
Both sit on the guideline's common, less discriminatory list; persistent hirsutism more often points to androgen excess (lesson 2.3).
Fatigue and poor sleep
Fatigue, insomnia and poor concentration are common and less discriminatory.
Eight sorted. Four features discriminate: easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal weakness and wide reddish-purple striae. A round face on its own is a weak signal.
The evidence
Rare, and usually from a prescription.

Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)
As cited in the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, 2008

A round, puffy face in an aesthetic clinic is almost always something other than Cushing's syndrome, and when cortisol excess is real it most often comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is already using.

It does not mean you can dismiss it. The guideline recommends testing when discriminating features are multiple and progressive or unusual for age, and some groups, such as people with poorly controlled diabetes, carry a higher rate.
What changes in practice
Reassure the many, refer the few.

When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.

First-line tests are urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol or an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, ordered by a prescriber; an abnormal result goes to an endocrinologist.

Lesson 2.2 · Concept
Estrogen and the dermis.

Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.

Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors in sun-protected and sun-damaged sites alike. In a vehicle-controlled study, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in the hip skin of postmenopausal women; in photoaged forearm and facial skin, the same treatment made no measurable difference. Small biopsy studies from the nineteen eighties and nineties found that skin collagen and thickness fall after menopause, and that the fall follows years since the last period more closely than birthdays. Keep two questions apart as you go. One is what estrogen does in the dermis. The other is whether giving it changes how a face ages, and those answers come from different trials.
Two panels of dermis: in sun-protected skin, receptor-bearing cells lay down new collagen; in sun-damaged skin, the same cells sit among fragmented, clumped fibres with no new collagen.

The evidence
One to two per cent a year.

In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.

Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. Where does that leave hormone therapy for skin? In the United States, as of February 2026, the approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products the prevention of bone loss. In late 2025 the FDA asked manufacturers to remove heart, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, and it approved the first revised labels in February 2026. Skin still appears nowhere among the uses. The menopause society's 2022 position statement finds the balance favourable for symptoms and bone when therapy starts before sixty or within ten years of menopause, and it finds too little evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms is the one use aimed at the tissue itself. For the face, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid carry better evidence than any hormone. Treat symptoms on their merits, and count any skin change as a bonus.

Prescribe hormone therapy for its labeled indications and the position statement's timing, and record that skin was discussed only as a secondary effect. Do not prescribe systemic or topical estrogen for wrinkles alone, and prefer licensed products (FDA-approved in the US) to compounded 'bioidentical' preparations.

If a patient asks for 'hormones for my skin', ask about hot flashes, sleep and vaginal symptoms, record what she says, and route those symptoms to the prescriber. The skin concern stays with skin-directed care.

In the US, a cream sold as containing estrogen for the face is regulated as a drug, and compounded 'bioidentical' products lack efficacy and safety data. Menopausal symptoms are a conversation for a prescriber; sun protection is advice you can give.

In the UK, as of September 2026, HRT products such as estradiol patches and gel are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis in women at high risk of fracture; skin is not among their uses. A compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine in the UK, and MHRA guidance puts a licensed product first when one can meet the need. On the UK medicines compendium, topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments.

In the EU, the harmonised core product information for HRT (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as its indications; skin is not an indication. EU cosmetics law prohibits oestrogens, progestogens and tretinoin in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II), and anti-wrinkle products containing tretinoin marketed as cosmetics are illegal cosmetics.

In Portugal, as of September 2026, the estradiol HRT products Estreva gel and Estrofem tablets are authorised for symptoms of oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women. The topical tretinoin product Ketrel cream is authorised and prescription-only on INFARMED's database, with indications for acne (except acne rosacea) and keratinisation disorders.

In Brazil, as of September 2026, estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy is registered and the Oestrogel label covers menopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, not skin ageing, while the Vitacid label for topical tretinoin names cutaneous photoageing as well as acne vulgaris. The Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) bars physicians from using hormones, in any formulation, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit (Resolution 1.999/2012), and from prescribing hormones marketed as 'bioidentical' or 'nano' without proof of superiority (Resolution 2.333/2023).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, registers estradiol products as Prescription Only Medicines, for example Oestrogel gel (since 11 November 2021). The EDE register lists therapeutic categories rather than indications, so it does not show whether any UAE label includes a skin indication (25 September 2026). Under the medicines law, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, a compounding pharmacy may not compound products that are essentially copies of EDE-approved products unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient.

Lesson 2.3 · Concept
Some syndromes show on the skin first.

A handful of inherited endocrine syndromes appear on the skin before the glands declare themselves. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common. In Carney complex, lentigines on the lips, eyelids and canthi, blue naevi and small skin myxomas sit alongside myxomas of the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN2A, an itchy, rippled, pigmented plaque between the shoulder blades can precede medullary thyroid cancer.
MEN1: facial angiofibromas, collagenomas
Carney complex: lip and eyelid lentigines, myxomas
MEN2A: lichen amyloidosis between the shoulder blades
MEN1
Loss of the tumour suppressor menin. Multiple facial angiofibromas, identical to those of tuberous sclerosis, and truncal collagenomas.
Carney complex
Inactivating variants in PRKAR1A, the regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. Lentigines, blue naevi and myxomas of skin and heart, with Cushing's syndrome from the adrenal.
MEN2A
Activating RET variants, most often at codon 634 when the skin is involved. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis over the upper back, often found before the thyroid cancer.

Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofibromas, the same lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis, along with collagenomas on the trunk. In Carney complex, usually caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene, freckle-like lentigines cluster on the lips, eyelids and the corners of the eyes, alongside blue naevi and small skin myxomas. The same patients can develop myxomas in the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN two A, an itchy, rippled, darkened patch between the shoulder blades, called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, can appear long before medullary thyroid cancer. Each of these is a referral finding, and none of them is yours to diagnose alone.

The evidence
Eighty-eight per cent.

In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.

It does not mean a single facial papule is MEN1. This is one small referral-centre series, and angiofibromas have other causes, tuberous sclerosis above all.
