The everyday endocrine signs.

Most endocrine skin signs you meet come from common disease. New generalised darkening, strongest in skin creases, scars, mucosa and sun-exposed skin, can signal primary adrenal insufficiency, which can turn into a life-threatening crisis. Hirsutism that appears fast, keeps progressing, or comes with a deepening voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely. Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance, pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease, and cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

Most of the endocrine skin signs you will actually meet come from common conditions. New, generalised darkening, most obvious in skin creases such as the palms, in scars, on the gums and on sun-exposed skin, can be the sign of primary adrenal insufficiency. In a patient who is also unwell, the Endocrine Society recommends testing, and a suspected adrenal crisis is treated before the results come back, because delay raises the risk of death. Hirsutism that arrives quickly, keeps progressing, or comes with a deeper voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely and calls for prompt referral. Velvety dark plaques in the neck folds track insulin resistance. Firm plaques on the shins point to Graves' disease, and cold, dry, coarse skin suggests an underactive thyroid. Module 03 · Opening film
Fat, incretins and the ageing face

Facial shape depends on fat as much as on collagen. In three lessons you will separate what is known about the skin's own fat, sugar damage to the dermis, weight-loss drugs and the gut from what is still mechanism, marketing or an open question. Most people picture skin fat as one layer under the dermis. There is a second, thinner layer inside the reticular dermis itself, called dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and its new fat cells release cathelicidin, an antimicrobial peptide. Older mice lose much of that capacity, through TGF-beta signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in small cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain preadipocytes around the follicle that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not yet been measured. So hold two things apart when you hear about skin fat. The defence story is strong in mice and emerging in people. The ageing story in people is still a proposal.
Mechanism
The skin keeps its own fat.

Beneath the dermis lies subcutaneous fat. Within the reticular dermis itself sits a thinner layer, dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, its new fat cells release the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin, and the capacity fades with age through TGF-β signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not been measured.
A second fat layer inside the dermis
In mice: antimicrobial, and lost with age
In people: a different shape, and an open question about ageing
A second fat layer
Dermal white adipose tissue sits inside the reticular dermis, separate from the subcutaneous fat below. Fat as a whole is an endocrine organ that releases hormones such as leptin and adiponectin.
What it does in mice
The layer expands after skin infection and its fat cells release cathelicidin. Older mice lose much of this capacity, through TGF-β signalling.
What is known in people
Human dermal fat clusters in cones around hair follicles, and acne lesions contain preadipocytes that make cathelicidin. Its part in skin ageing is unmeasured.

Human evidence
Fat that holds the face up.

Cadaver dissection shows that the face's subcutaneous fat sits in separate compartments, and facial ageing is partly how each compartment changes. Weight shows the same thing from the outside. In a study of 186 pairs of identical twins, the twin with the higher body-mass index looked older before about age 40 and younger after it.
pairs of identical twins compared for facial ageing
Guyuron et al., 2009 — a four-point higher BMI tracked with an older look before about 40 and a younger look after it
From midlife on, facial fat goes with a younger-looking face. That fits the anatomy: the face ages partly as its fat compartments change. GRADE C, observational.
It is an observational comparison of photographs. It does not show that gaining weight rejuvenates, or that fat loss on a drug changes the skin itself.
Mechanism
Sugar that sticks to collagen.

Glycation is a slow, non-enzymatic reaction. Reducing sugars attach to protein amino groups, rearrange into Amadori products and end as advanced glycation end products, or AGEs. On long-lived dermal collagen, AGEs form cross-links that stiffen the matrix. Through their receptor, RAGE, AGEs switch on inflammatory signalling in laboratory studies. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects B; the course grades the causal link to visible ageing D, because the human data are associations.
Sugar + protein → Schiff base → Amadori product → AGE
Cross-links stiffen long-lived collagen
RAGE signalling: shown in the laboratory
The reaction
Reducing sugars bind protein amino groups, form a reversible Schiff base, then a more stable Amadori product, and finally irreversible AGEs.
Two kinds of damage
Structural: AGEs cross-link collagen and elastin and stiffen the dermis. Signalling: AGEs bind RAGE, which drives NF-κB and inflammatory cytokines in cell and animal studies.
Where the grades differ
The Hormonaly endocrinology guide rates both B. The course grades the causal link to visible ageing D, because the human data are associations.

Glycation is chemistry before it is biology. Reducing sugars attach to the amino groups of proteins, rearrange into more stable products, and end as advanced glycation end products, known as AGEs. Dermal collagen lasts for years, so it collects AGEs, and they form cross-links that make the matrix stiffer. AGEs also bind a receptor called RAGE, which in laboratory studies switches on inflammatory signalling and enzymes that break down matrix. Keep the registers apart here. The chemistry, and the build-up of AGEs in human skin, are well documented. The idea that AGEs cause the wrinkles and laxity you see in clinic rests on laboratory and animal work plus human associations. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects grade B. This course grades the causal link D, and the next moment shows why.
On the left, parallel collagen fibres lie free; on the right, the same fibres carry small sugar rings and are tied together by short cross-links.

Human evidence
Fifteen years on the same collagen.

Human skin collagen turns over slowly; tissue analysis puts its half-life at about 15 years. In skin biopsies, glycoxidation products in collagen rose about five-fold between ages 20 and 85, and were up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes. Skin autofluorescence, a non-invasive reading, correlates moderately with those biopsy measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin.
estimated half-life of human skin collagen
Verzijl et al., 2000 · AGE content of skin collagen rises about five-fold from age 20 to 85 (Dyer et al., 1993)
Glycation damage accumulates on the same collagen for years, and faster with higher glucose exposure. That much is measured in human skin: direct, observational, GRADE C.
It does not show how much of visible ageing AGEs cause, or that any product reverses established cross-links. Skin autofluorescence is a surrogate reading of AGE load.

Lesson 3.2 · Concept
Two gut hormones, re-engineered.

GLP-1 and GIP are incretins, hormones the gut releases after a meal that amplify glucose-dependent insulin release; GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 is broken down within minutes. Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist, and tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In the US, as of September 2026, both are FDA-approved drugs for defined indications, set out in the next moment.
Incretins amplify insulin after meals
Semaglutide: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Tirzepatide: GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist
Incretins
GLP-1 from intestinal L-cells and GIP from K-cells amplify insulin release when glucose is high. GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite.
Engineered to last
Native GLP-1 is cleared within minutes by the enzyme DPP-4. The drug molecules are modified to last far longer in the blood.
Two molecules, four brands
In the US, semaglutide is sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, tirzepatide as Mounjaro and Zepbound, and the brand tells you the approved use.

After a meal, the gut releases two hormones called incretins, GLP-1 and GIP. Both amplify insulin release when glucose is high, and GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood before an enzyme breaks it down, so the drug molecules are engineered to last far longer. Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide activates both the GIP and the GLP-1 receptors. Those are the mechanisms. The regulatory facts sit in a separate register. In the United States, as of September 2026, both molecules are FDA-approved drugs, sold under one brand name for type 2 diabetes and another for chronic weight management, with further indications for the heart, the liver and sleep apnoea. The face appears nowhere on those labels, and that is where this lesson begins.
In the UK both are licensed by the MHRA, and tirzepatide's diabetes and weight-management uses share one brand, Mounjaro.

In the EU, semaglutide is a centrally authorised prescription medicine, as Ozempic and Rybelsus for diabetes and Wegovy for weight management (EMA and HMA, June 2024), and tirzepatide is authorised as Mounjaro (EU-wide, 15 September 2022) for diabetes and adult weight management, prescription-only. A search of the Union Register and EMA's medicines data on 25 September 2026 found no EU product named Zepbound.

In Brazil, ANVISA has registered semaglutide as Ozempic (since 6 August 2018) and Wegovy (since 2 January 2023), with synthetic semaglutide pens registered from 26 May 2026, and tirzepatide as Mounjaro (since 25 September 2023); a search of its register on 25 September 2026 found no product named Zepbound. Since 23 June 2025, GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines may only be sold with retention of the prescription (RDC 973/2025 and IN 360/2025).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and its register lists semaglutide as Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy and tirzepatide as Mounjaro; every entry checked is a Prescription Only Medicine. A search of the EDE register on 25 September 2026 found no product named Zepbound.

In the UK (MHRA, September 2026), Ozempic is licensed for diabetes and Mounjaro for diabetes and weight. Human evidence
Large trials, measured on the scale.

In STEP-1, 1,961 adults without diabetes lost a mean 14.9% of body weight on semaglutide over 68 weeks, against 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1, 2,539 adults lost 15.0% to 20.9% on tirzepatide over 72 weeks, depending on dose, against 3.1% on placebo. Both Hormonaly guides grade weight management A. Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue.
mean weight loss in STEP-1 (semaglutide, 68 weeks) and SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide, highest dose, 72 weeks)
Placebo 2.4% and 3.1% · both trials industry-funded, both the basis for approval

These drugs produce large, reproducible weight loss in randomized trials: GRADE A for the approved indications. Part of what is lost is lean tissue, which is why the Hormonaly guide pairs treatment with protein and resistance training.
Neither pivotal trial measured facial fat, skin laxity or appearance. An A for weight loss says nothing about the face.
Four registers
'Ozempic face', answer by answer.
The phrase bundles four kinds of statement. Kept apart, they tell a patient far more than the headline does.
Mechanism
Volume loss
Losing fat deflates the superficial facial compartments and unmasks laxity that was already there.
Human evidence
Observational and small: C to D

One imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial, about 7% per 10 kg lost. A survey of 1,226 patients found sagging, facial volume loss and hair shedding reported more often the more weight was lost. A systematic review of the plastic-surgery literature found it limited by study bias. No randomized trial has measured the face.
Regulatory status (US, September 2026)
Hair loss labelled; facial change unlisted

Both labels list hair loss (about 3–6% on drug against about 1% on placebo, mostly in women, linked to weight reduction). The semaglutide label also lists altered skin sensation. Facial volume loss is not a labelled adverse reaction.
Open question
A direct drug effect?
Whether these drugs act on facial fat or skin cells beyond the effect of weight loss rests on cell studies and has not been tested in people.
So far, the evidence ties facial change to how much weight is lost.
UK product information also lists hair loss: 2.5% on Wegovy and 4.9% on Mounjaro in the weight-management trials, against 1.0% on placebo.

What changes in practice
Counsel before, record during, refer when asked.

Raise facial volume change and hair shedding before treatment starts; the Hormonaly guide advises this especially for older patients. During treatment, photograph the face with consent, and support the protein intake and resistance training the guide recommends to protect lean mass. When a patient wants the face restored, refer to a qualified aesthetic or dermatology colleague. Published advice on restoration is expert opinion, the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement, and randomized trials of fillers and devices in these patients are registered without results. Decisions about the medicine itself stay with the prescriber and the patient.

Say nothing yet; raise the face if she notices a change.
The guide's advice is to raise facial volume change and hair shedding before treatment starts, especially with older patients, and to record that you did.
Months into treatment, she is losing weight steadily. What do you add at follow-up?
Consented photographs of her face, and support for protein intake and resistance training.

Right. Photographs mean change is measured rather than remembered, and the guide recommends protein intake and resistance training to protect lean mass: across 35 randomized trials, a median of about 28% of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue.
Nothing beyond her weight; that is what the trials measured.
Weight is only part of what changes. Part of what is lost is lean tissue, which is why the Hormonaly guide pairs treatment with protein and resistance training.
Ask at each visit whether her face looks different to her.
Memory is not a record. Photograph the face with consent, so that change is measured rather than remembered.
Later, she asks you to restore the volume in her cheeks. What do you do?
Refer her to a qualified aesthetic or dermatology colleague, and tell her that advice on restoration is still expert opinion.

Right. Published advice on restoration is expert opinion, the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement, and randomized trials of fillers and devices in these patients are registered without results.
Tell her randomized trials show that fillers restore the face after drug-driven weight loss.
They have not reported: randomized trials of fillers and devices in these patients are registered without results, and published advice is expert opinion.
Improvise a restoration plan yourself at today's visit.
Refer restoration requests rather than improvising them; the guidance is to refer to a qualified aesthetic or dermatology colleague.
Document each stage as you go: what you raised before treatment, the consented photographs and the referral.
Counsel before, record during, refer when asked, and leave decisions about the medicine itself to the prescriber and the patient.

Lesson 3.3 · Concept
Inflammation that comes with age.

Inflammaging is the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age. In older adults, higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty and death. One proposed source is the gut. In mice, a high-fat diet raises circulating bacterial lipopolysaccharide, and infusing it reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance. Inflammaging
A slow rise in background inflammation with age. Higher IL-6 and CRP predict frailty, disability and death in older adults.
The gut hypothesis
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide crossing a leaky barrier is one proposed source, shown in mice and as a short rise after a fatty meal in a small human study.
Where the evidence stops
Measuring gut permeability is hard, and restoring the barrier has not been shown to improve disease outside the gut.

Ageing brings a slow rise in background inflammation, called inflammaging. It is low-grade and sterile, and in older adults higher IL-6 and C-reactive protein predict frailty, disability and death. One proposed source is the gut. In mice, a high-fat diet raises bacterial lipopolysaccharide in the blood, and infusing that endotoxin reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance. In twelve healthy men, a single high-fat meal raised plasma endotoxin within four hours. That is the mechanism usually called metabolic endotoxaemia, or leaky gut. The human evidence stops short of the skin. Measuring gut permeability is difficult, and a leading review concludes that it is still unproven whether restoring the barrier improves disease outside the gut. Hold that line as you look at what patients are sold.
Two views of the gut lining: one with closed junctions keeping small bacterial fragments out, the other with loosened junctions letting them pass into a blood vessel.
The evidence
Thirty-nine trials of probiotics for eczema.

An independent Cochrane review pooled 39 randomized trials, with 2,599 participants, of oral probiotics for eczema. Probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated symptoms, and investigator-rated severity fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference. A 2024 European task-force meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported a significant fall in severity scores.
in the Cochrane review of oral probiotics for treating eczema
2,599 participants · little or no difference in patient-rated symptoms (moderate-certainty evidence)
The most direct test of 'treat the gut, help the skin' in a common inflammatory skin disease shows, at most, a small effect. GRADE B for little or no benefit a patient would notice.
It does not rule out benefit from particular strains or in particular groups, and it says nothing about skin ageing. Newer pooled analyses in children report small improvements.

Patients often link their skin to their gut. Start where the evidence is. Diet quality, treatment of metabolic disease and the established treatment for the skin condition itself all come first. Be careful with tests. A widely used commercial zonulin assay was shown to detect proteins other than zonulin, so a result cannot tell you whether a gut is leaky. Be careful with products too. Probiotics are strain-specific, and their effects on eczema are small at best. The Hormonaly guide gives the popular gut-repair stack of glutamine, zinc carnosine and BPC-157 a grade of D. As of September 2026, in the United States, BPC-157 remains off the 503A bulks list after the July advisory-committee review. Investigational peptides come last, if at all. Whatever your role, name the evidence type before you name the product.

Treat the skin disease on its own evidence and metabolic disease directly. A zonulin result should not guide care. In the US, BPC-157 has no 503A bulks-list standing as of September 2026, so compounding it for gut repair is not an option.
If a patient brings a gut-repair kit or a zonulin result, record the products and the result and bring them to the prescriber. Do not interpret the test or advise on the products.

You can say that fibre-rich diets have strong evidence for metabolic health, that probiotics are strain-specific with small skin effects at best, and that injected or research peptides need a prescriber.
In the United Kingdom, an unlicensed peptide reaches a patient only through narrow routes, such as a special ordered for one patient's clinical need, which module seven sets out.

In the EU, Directive 2001/83/EC allows a medicine on the market only with a national or EU-wide marketing authorisation (Article 6(1)), while medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formulas) fall outside the directive and need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3). Each member state may also, under its own law, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, no medicine containing BPC-157 is listed in INFARMED's Infomed register (25 September 2026). A medicine is defined as any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease or that may be used or administered to restore, correct, or modify physiological functions through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento, Article 3). INFARMED does not authorise importing medicines for personal use, and a compounded medicine may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese Pharmacopoeia, the European Pharmacopoeia, pharmacopoeias of other States Parties to the European Pharmacopoeia Convention, or compendial scientific documentation (Decreto-Lei 95/2004, Article 6).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that any substance must have undergone efficacy and safety assessments before it can be compounded, and that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or food supplement) and are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use. ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used exclusively in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, in force since 2 January 2025, bars importing, selling or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), and lets a physician prescribe a medicine never submitted for approval only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any research-use peptide on humans, or for treatment, outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH lets physicians prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status, and compounded peptides may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight (31 July 2026).

Module 04 · Opening film
Matrix peptides and wound healing

Most skin peptides reach your clinic before any evidence does. In three lessons you will sort them by what the human trials actually show, who paid for those trials, and where each one stands with the regulator. Start with the molecule. GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide that circulates in human plasma; it was first described in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex, GHK-Cu, is what skin-care labels mean when they say copper peptide. The proposed mechanism is that GHK-Cu delivers copper to enzymes that build and protect the dermal matrix, such as lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase, and shifts gene expression toward wound healing. Two things to hold on to. First, this is a mechanism, which explains why the peptide might work and leaves open whether it does. Second, most of this literature was written by the group that discovered the peptide. Keep both in mind when you reach the trials.

Mechanism
A plasma tripeptide with a copper habit.

GHK is a tripeptide found in human plasma, first described in 1973. Bound to copper it becomes GHK-Cu, which is proposed to deliver copper to enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and to switch on wound-healing and antioxidant gene programmes. Most of that mechanistic literature comes from the group that discovered the peptide.
Endogenous: GHK circulates in human plasma
Proposed: copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes
Mechanism register only — written largely by the originator
Where it comes from
GHK — glycyl-histidyl-lysine — was isolated from human plasma in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex is what the skin-care literature calls GHK-Cu.
What it is proposed to do
The proposed mechanism is copper delivery to enzymes that build and protect the matrix, plus broad changes in gene expression linked to wound healing.
Who wrote it
Much of this work, including the gene-expression reviews, comes from the peptide's discoverer. That does not make it wrong. It does make it a mechanism, and it is worth saying who proposed it.

Human evidence
One indexed randomized trial.

A search of PubMed in September 2026 found one randomized controlled trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin: 2006, healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing. The cosmetic trials cited for anti-ageing claims are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed. Both Hormonaly guides grade topical use C.

Miller et al., 2006 — healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing, not photoageing
The human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small: one small indexed trial plus sponsor-run cosmetic studies. GRADE C is the honest ceiling.
It does not show that GHK-Cu fails, that it treats photoageing, or anything about injecting it. A thin evidence base is an unknown, not a negative.
Four registers
Keep the four answers apart.
Every peptide question has four separate answers. For GHK-Cu they point in different directions, which is exactly why they must not be blended into one sentence.
Mechanism
Plausible
Copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes; gene-expression data from the originator

Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating and does not intend to act against compounders who meet its conditions; an advisory-committee consultation is planned before the end of February 2027. The injectable route has no such standing.

Does it reach the dermis?
Penetration data are in vitro and depend on how they are measured

Here is what that means in the room. Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation, as long as you describe the evidence honestly: small trials, modest effects, grade C. Injected GHK-Cu is not the same product in a stronger form. There are no randomized trials of injection, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the United States the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing that covers non-injectable use. Whatever your role, name the route every time you talk about this peptide.

In the US, before prescribing a compounded topical, confirm the substance's current 503A status and that the pharmacy is working within it. Do not prescribe GHK-Cu for injection. Record that you discussed a product with small-trial evidence and the patient's reasons for choosing it.
If a patient tells you they inject GHK-Cu, record the product, where it was bought and any site reactions, and bring it to the prescriber. Do not advise on amounts or technique.
Describe topical GHK-Cu products as cosmetics with modest, small-trial support. Anyone injecting a copper peptide should be pointed to a prescriber, not to a better supplier.

In the UK, anything injected falls outside cosmetics law, and MHRA decides whether it is a medicine from its claims, form and use. In the UK, a GHK-Cu serum presented for appearance is a cosmetic, so there is nothing to prescribe.

In the EU, a substance or mixture intended to be injected is not considered a cosmetic product (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)); the EU borderline manual adds that a product in a vial or ampoule for use by injection cannot be considered a cosmetic product, and should not be marketed with a device that could allow injection or delivery below the epidermis. Whether a product qualifies as a cosmetic is decided case by case by national competent authorities, and the manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as one (version 5.5, June 2025).

In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by injection are not considered cosmetics (as of 25 September 2026), and medicines intended for parenteral administration are subject to medical prescription by law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 114(1)(d)).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist; an injectable product offered as a cosmetic is irregular. Products with 'GHK' in the product name appear as notified cosmetics in ANVISA's public cosmetics data (221 entries, 25 September 2026), and ANVISA cancelled several GHK-Cu cosmetic processes on 29 April 2026 without published reasons (RE 1.771/2026).

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) defines cosmetics as products with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and whether a product requires an Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) marketing authorisation, and in which category, is determined by an EDE classification letter based on its presentation, composition, use and design. In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed health facility (DHA, 29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (DoH, 31 July 2026).

Lesson 4.2 · Concept
Three families, one question: who ran the trial?

Signal peptides such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS, Matrixyl) are meant to tell fibroblasts to make matrix. SNAP-25 mimics (Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8) and Leuphasyl, an enkephalin analogue, are meant to quieten expression lines. Oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. All three families have a trial record, and in all three the question that matters most is who funded it.

Signal peptides
Palmitoylated fragments of matrix proteins, designed to mimic the signals that tell fibroblasts to repair. The palmitoyl tail helps them into the skin.
SNAP-25 mimics
Argireline copies the end of SNAP-25, a protein botulinum toxin cleaves. SNAP-8 is the maker's eight-residue extension. The premise is a gentler topical version of the same effect.
Oral collagen
Hydrolysed collagen taken by mouth, sold as a supplement, with more randomized trials than any topical peptide — and the clearest funding problem.

Lesson two covers three families that fill the cosmetic and supplement shelves. Signal peptides, like palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl, are fragments of matrix proteins meant to tell fibroblasts to make more collagen. SNAP-25 mimics, Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8, copy part of a nerve-terminal protein that botulinum toxin targets; the idea is a gentle, topical version of that effect. And oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. Every one of these has trials behind it. As you go through them, keep asking one question before any other: who ran the trial, and who paid for it.

What changes in practice
Cosmetic, supplement, drug: three rulebooks.

In the US, cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework. Oral collagen is a dietary supplement: it may not claim to treat disease, and product quality and content vary. Neither route has to prove efficacy before sale — which is why the funding question matters.
Cosmetic ingredient: no efficacy approval needed
Dietary supplement: no disease claims; quality varies
Say 'modest, small-trial' — never 'topical Botox'

Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub varies from brand to brand. That is the whole reason the funding question matters here. When no regulator asks for efficacy, the only efficacy data are the trials someone chose to pay for.
Nothing here needs a prescription. If you recommend a product, recommend it on evidence, name the grade, and disclose any relationship with the brand. The 'topical Botox' claim is not one to repeat.
When a patient asks which serum 'really works', the accurate answer is modest effects from mostly sponsor-funded trials. Do not describe any of them as an alternative to botulinum toxin.

The claim you can stand behind is modest, small-trial evidence. Supplements cannot be sold as treating a disease; if a patient expects collagen to fix a skin condition, that is a conversation for a prescriber.

In the UK, a peptide serum is a cosmetic: its responsible person needs a safety assessment and must notify the regulator before sale, and must be able to prove its claims. Oral collagen is a food supplement: no food may claim to prevent, treat or cure disease, and only authorised health claims may be used. In May 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled a peptide serum's 'clinically proven' lifting claim misleading because the study behind it was small and uncontrolled.

In the EU, a peptide serum sold as a cosmetic needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a product safety report and electronic notification to the Commission before it is placed on the market (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009), and its claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013). Food labelling and advertising may not claim that a food prevents, treats or cures a disease, and health claims on foods are prohibited unless authorised: the Commission refused a claim that a collagen peptide mixture maintains skin health by increasing elasticity and reducing wrinkles, because cause and effect was not established (Regulation (EU) No 1154/2014), and the EU Register lists no authorised claim for collagen itself (searched 25 September 2026).

In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics (Decreto-Lei 23/2025), and borderline products must be assessed case by case by the Responsible Person, taking all their characteristics into account (INFARMED, as of 25 September 2026). For food supplement notification, there is no evaluation of the product or validation of labelling; control is carried out afterwards by sampling and may take place at any time (DGAV, as of 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling must not contain trade names, brands, images, electronic links or wording that represent therapeutic claims attributed to the use of the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12). Under ANVISA's January 2025 food supplement guidance, an approved claim is that bioactive hydrolysed collagen peptides with an average molecular weight of 2 kDa help maintain skin health.

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) treats food supplements, oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease, as medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE): oral collagen products are registered with the EDE as general-sale-list health products rather than medicines, while ordinary cosmetics need a conformity certificate from the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014. Advertising any medical product, social media included, requires EDE approval. In Dubai, the DHA's rules for health facilities ban misleading or unproven peptide claims, such as anti-ageing, cell regeneration or improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status (29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, the DoH bars healthcare providers from promoting peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertising them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (31 July 2026).

A synthetic 15-residue peptide first described in 1993. Decades of rodent studies, most from one Zagreb group; in people, uncontrolled case series.

Lesson three moves from the cosmetic shelf to the peptides patients buy online and inject. BPC-157 is a fifteen-residue peptide first described in 1993. Its evidence is a large rodent literature, most of it from one research group, and uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is sold as thymosin, but when anti-doping chemists analysed the product they found a seven-residue fragment, residues seventeen to twenty-three of thymosin beta-four. That fragment has never been tested in a trial. KPV is the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH; it calms inflammation in mouse colitis models, and there is no randomized human trial of it for anything. All three have plausible mechanisms, and none has a controlled human trial.
A mouse on a lab plinth, a long peptide chain with a short fragment lifted out, and a shorter chain with its last three beads set apart.
The evidence
One abstract, no published trial.

As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published in full. FDA's July 2026 briefing found one randomized, placebo-controlled trial reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, two weeks of treatment, and no significant difference from placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov adds a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, and a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff surgery due to start in 2027.
randomized efficacy trials of BPC-157 in people published in full (September 2026)

One 2005 ulcerative-colitis trial exists only as a meeting abstract (no significant difference from placebo) · registered: phase 1 safety study (2015, no results) · single-arm product study (2025, no results) · randomized phase 1 after rotator-cuff repair (starts 2027)
Whether BPC-157 helps people heal is unknown. The only randomized human result is an abstract that showed no significant benefit; the enthusiasm rests on rodents and uncontrolled case series.
It does not show BPC-157 is ineffective or unsafe. Absence of trials is absence of evidence, and this figure will change when the registered trials report.

If you practise in the UK, the route for unlicensed medicines works differently, and lesson 7.2 sets it out.

In the EU, a medicine prepared in a pharmacy on prescription for an individual patient (magistral formula), or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula), falls outside Directive 2001/83/EC and needs no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3), and each member state may, under its own law, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a professional's bona fide unsolicited order, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)). Compounded medicines may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese pharmacopoeia, the European pharmacopoeia or another European pharmacopoeia, or in compendial scientific documentation, and one containing any other raw material may not be prescribed.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that any substance must have passed efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded, and that compounding may only be individual, on presentation of a medical prescription, by a compounding pharmacy licensed by local health surveillance. The same notice says BPC-157 and TB-500 are not authorised as food supplements, and that products presented as peptides called GHK-CU, BPC-157, and TB-500 promising aesthetic effects or health improvements are not registered with ANVISA.

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, in force 2 January 2025) exempts medical products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies from the requirement for a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE). In Dubai, the DHA's rules for health facilities prohibit circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering or using any peptide product unless it is registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026); in Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances, and novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine or listed on the DoH's register of compounded substances (compounding standard, August 2026).

ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used exclusively in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, the medicines law (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024) has, since 2 January 2025, barred importing, distributing, possessing, selling, using or manufacturing any medical product for circulation without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), and no registered medical product matching GHK-Cu, BPC-157 or TB-500 was found in the EDE register (25 September 2026). In Dubai, the DHA's rules for health facilities prohibit using any peptide product intended for research use on humans, or for therapeutic purposes, outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority, and bar buying, accepting or using peptide products from websites, social media, individual accounts or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH requires compounded peptide formulations to use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight, with peptide products traceable from source to patient (31 July 2026).

Module 05 · Opening film
Follicle, pigment and melanocortins

Two requests reach aesthetic clinics well ahead of their evidence: a peptide to regrow hair and an injection to tan. In three lessons you will see how the follicle and the pigment system run on the skin's own hormones, why one melanocortin drug is approved while its gray-market cousin is approved nowhere, and how to grade the hair peptides patients bring to you. Each hair follicle behaves like a small gland. When researchers keep human scalp follicles alive in culture, the follicles answer corticotropin-releasing hormone the way the pituitary and adrenal glands do. They make ACTH and alpha-MSH, they secrete cortisol, and cortisol-like signals feed back to switch the stimulus down. On the scalp, an enzyme called five-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, and in genetically susceptible follicles that hormone drives the gradual shrinking behind pattern hair loss. Most of this biology comes from tissue kept alive outside the body, so hold it as mechanism, a reason something might matter in patients.
Mechanism
A follicle that runs its own hormones.

Human scalp hair follicles kept alive in the laboratory answer corticotropin-releasing hormone by making ACTH and α-MSH and secreting cortisol, with a feedback loop like the adrenal axis. They also run a growth hormone and IGF-1 loop of their own. Locally made dihydrotestosterone shrinks genetically susceptible scalp follicles, the process behind pattern hair loss. Growing follicles are shielded from immune attack, and alopecia areata begins when that shield fails.
Local stress axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Local androgen switch: testosterone → DHT in the scalp
Immune privilege: its collapse drives alopecia areata
Its own stress axis
Organ-cultured human scalp follicles respond to CRH by making POMC products and secreting cortisol, and hydrocortisone in turn damps follicular CRH, the adrenal axis in miniature.
Its own growth and androgen signals
Outside the body, follicles also run a GH and IGF-1 loop. In susceptible scalp follicles, locally made DHT drives the miniaturisation of pattern hair loss.
Hidden from the immune system
Growing follicles show little antigen to immune cells. When that privilege collapses, T cells and natural killer cells attack the bulb and alopecia areata follows.

Human evidence
Two trials, 1,200 adults, one approval.

When immune privilege fails, the attack depends on cytokine signals that JAK inhibitors interrupt. Two randomized phase 3 trials tested oral baricitinib in 1,200 adults with severe alopecia areata. In the US, FDA approved baricitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata on 13 June 2022. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades it A.
adults with severe alopecia areata in the two phase 3 trials of baricitinib (2022)
At 36 weeks, up to 39% of patients on baricitinib had at least 80% of their scalp hair, against 3–6% on placebo
Interrupting the immune signalling behind collapsed privilege regrows hair in severe alopecia areata. That is approval-grade evidence (A), and it shows what real follicle evidence looks like.
It says nothing about pattern hair loss, cosmetic thinning or any peptide. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer, and the authors called for longer trials.
In the UK, baricitinib is licensed for severe alopecia areata in adults, and NICE did not recommend it for NHS use in October 2023, on cost-effectiveness.

In the EU, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been centrally authorised since 13 February 2017; its indications include severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over, and it is prescription-only, started by a doctor experienced in the condition (EMA). Since EMA's January 2023 review, JAK inhibitors including Olumiant should be used in people aged 65 or over, at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk, or long-term smokers only if no suitable alternative exists, and this applies to alopecia areata.
In Portugal, Olumiant (baricitinib) is classified as a restricted-prescription medicine (MSRM restrita - Alínea a), according to INFARMED's Infomed register on 25 September 2026.

In Brazil, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been registered by ANVISA since 26 November 2018, and its current label includes severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 or over weighing at least 30 kg (checked 25 September 2026).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. The EDE register lists Olumiant (baricitinib) tablets, registered since 8 June 2017, as Prescription Only and files them under rheumatic diseases; it does not show whether alopecia areata is an approved UAE indication (25 September 2026).

Work up the hair loss before anyone mentions a peptide.

Pattern, trigger, patches and androgens decide the treatment. Pooled randomized trials support topical minoxidil in men and women and finasteride in men. In the US, as of September 2026, topical minoxidil is FDA-approved and sold over the counter, finasteride for pattern hair loss is a prescription drug, and baricitinib is approved for adults with severe alopecia areata.

Most requests for a hair peptide skip the diagnosis. Start with the pattern, ask about a trigger, look for patches and nail pitting, and look for signs of androgen excess. Check ferritin and thyroid function every time, and send a scarring pattern for biopsy. The approved options already carry strong evidence. Pooled randomized trials support topical minoxidil in men and women and finasteride in men. In the United States minoxidil is sold over the counter, while finasteride for hair loss needs a prescription. Severe or fast-spreading alopecia areata belongs with a dermatologist, where a JAK inhibitor is an approved option for adults. Whatever your role, the workup comes before the product.

Complete the workup and record the pattern before prescribing. Offer the approved options with their grades, refer severe or rapidly progressive alopecia areata, and document any investigational product the patient raises and what you advised. In the UK, before prescribing finasteride, ask about any history of depression, give the patient card, and review mood and sexual side effects.
Note the pattern, the timeline and any recent trigger, photograph the scalp with consent if your setting allows, and pass it to the prescriber. Patchy or fast-spreading loss needs prompt escalation.

In the UK, topical minoxidil is licensed and a men's foam is on general sale, finasteride for hair loss is available only on private prescription, and baricitinib is licensed for severe alopecia areata in adults. In May 2026 MHRA strengthened its warnings that finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction that may persist after stopping.

In the EU, topical minoxidil is authorised nationally, finasteride tablets and a finasteride skin spray are authorised in various member states for early androgenetic alopecia in men aged 18 to 41 (EMA, 2025), and baricitinib (Olumiant) is centrally authorised and prescription-only, with severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over among its indications. After an EU-wide review endorsed on 19 June 2025, suicidal ideation is a confirmed side effect of finasteride tablets, and packs of the hair-loss tablets carry a patient card.

In Brazil, minoxidil products such as Aloxidil are indicated for androgenetic alopecia in adult men, and finasteride products such as Pro Hair are indicated for the treatment of men with male-pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia). Lesson 5.2 · Concept
Five receptors, one family of hormones.

Skin makes proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and cuts it into ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. Those peptides act on five melanocortin receptors. MC1R drives pigment in skin and hair, MC2R answers ACTH in the adrenal gland, MC3R and MC4R act in the brain on appetite, and MC5R governs sebum. Which receptors a drug reaches decides what else it does.
MC1R: pigment of skin and hair
MC2R: adrenal · MC5R: sebum
MC3R and MC4R: appetite, in the brain
Made in the skin
Skin cells make POMC and cut it into ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin, and they carry the receptors that answer them.
Five receptors
MC1R pigment, MC2R adrenal, MC3R and MC4R appetite in the brain, MC5R sebum. Reviewers note the real distribution is probably wider than this tidy map.
Selectivity is the safety story
A drug that stays on MC1R mostly changes pigment. A drug that reaches the brain's receptors brings nausea, appetite loss and erections with it.

Pigment starts with hormones the skin makes for itself. Skin cells produce a precursor called POMC and cut it into ACTH, alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin, and the same cells carry the receptors that answer them. There are five melanocortin receptors. MC1R sets the pigment of skin and hair. MC2R is the adrenal receptor for ACTH. MC3R and MC4R work in the brain on appetite, and central receptors also drive sexual responses. MC5R governs sebum. Researchers caution that the real map is messier, with receptors turning up in more tissues than the textbook suggests. For this lesson one idea matters most. A drug that stays on MC1R mostly changes pigment, and a drug that reaches the brain's receptors brings other effects with it.

Four registers
One receptor family, two very different molecules.
Afamelanotide and Melanotan II are both synthetic relatives of α-MSH. Compare them register by register and the resemblance ends at the receptor.
Mechanism
Afamelanotide: MC1R agonist · Melanotan II: non-selective
Melanotan II also acts on MC3R, MC4R and MC5R and reaches the brain
Human evidence
Afamelanotide: A, for EPP only · Melanotan II: D

Two phase 3 trials in erythropoietic protoporphyria, against a three-volunteer pilot and a ten-man erectile-dysfunction study from the 1990s. The Peptide Pocket Guide rates Melanotan II C and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide D; with no trial of tanning, this course uses D.

Afamelanotide is approved only for EPP, as the manufacturer's implant. Melanotan II is approved for no indication anywhere.
Open question
Uses beyond EPP; melanoma risk
A phase 3 trial of afamelanotide in vitiligo began in 2023 and has posted no results. Whether Melanotan II causes melanoma is unproven.
A shared receptor does not bring a shared approval.
In the UK, afamelanotide is licensed under exceptional circumstances and prescribed only in specialist porphyria centres, and NICE did not recommend it for NHS use (July 2023).

In the EU, afamelanotide (Scenesse implant) is authorised for erythropoietic protoporphyria, under exceptional circumstances (European Commission, 22 December 2014), and is prescribed only by specialists in recognised EPP centres.

In Portugal, Scenesse is authorised through the EU procedure but classified as a restricted-prescription medicine for exclusive hospital use (MSRM restrita, alínea a), and no presentation is marketed in Portugal (INFARMED's Infomed register, 25 September 2026).

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing afamelanotide (Scenesse) was found: ANVISA's open-data register and its online medicines search returned no match on 25 September 2026, and the substance is absent from ANVISA's substance dictionary.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. An ingredient and product-name search of the EDE register found no registered product containing afamelanotide, and none named Scenesse (25 September 2026).
The evidence
Sixty-nine hours against forty-one.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is a rare disorder in which sunlight causes acute, severe pain. In the US phase 3 trial, adults on afamelanotide spent a median 69.4 hours in direct sunlight without pain over six months, against 40.8 hours on placebo. The European trial also showed more pain-free time and fewer phototoxic reactions. Both trials were funded by the manufacturer.
median pain-free hours in direct sunlight over six months, afamelanotide vs placebo (US phase 3 trial, 94 adults with EPP)
Langendonk et al., NEJM 2015 · European trial, 74 adults: 6.0 vs 0.8 hours over nine months
Afamelanotide lets people with EPP spend more time in sunlight without pain. That is approval-grade evidence (A) for one rare disease.
It says nothing about cosmetic tanning, about Melanotan II, or about unsupervised injections. Even in EPP, the US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice a year.
Safety signals
What the case reports show.

The harms of Melanotan II come from case reports and reviews, so they show what can happen without telling you how often. Reported skin effects include darkening and growth of existing moles, crops of new and sometimes atypical naevi, and dark bands in the nails. At least five melanomas have been reported during or after use, each in someone with other risk factors, so causation is unproven. Systemic reports include ischaemic priapism needing surgery and a stimulant-like toxic reaction with rhabdomyolysis, and FDA lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious events.
Skin: changing moles, eruptive naevi, melanonychia
Melanoma: reported, causation unproven
Systemic: priapism, rhabdomyolysis, encephalopathy
Moles and nails
Existing moles darken and grow, new naevi appear in crops, some atypical on histology, and nails can develop dark bands. In one report the new naevi faded after the injections stopped.
Melanoma, a signal without proof
At least five melanomas have been reported during or after use. Every patient had other risk factors, such as fair skin, sunbed use or a family history.
The rest of the body
Nausea, flushing and yawning are common. Reported emergencies include ischaemic priapism needing surgery, rhabdomyolysis with kidney injury, and encephalopathy.

Now the harms, and the kind of evidence behind them. Everything here comes from case reports and reviews, which tell you what can happen and leave open how often it does. In the skin, existing moles darken and grow, new moles erupt in crops, some of them atypical under the microscope, and dark bands can appear in the nails. At least five melanomas have been reported during or after Melanotan use. Each patient had other risk factors, such as fair skin, sunbed use or a family history, so causation is unproven, and the concern rests on a drug that pushes melanocytes to multiply. Beyond the skin, reports describe priapism that needed surgery, a stimulant-like toxic reaction with muscle breakdown and kidney injury, and a brain swelling syndrome that FDA lists among the published serious events.

Lesson 5.3 · Concept
A Wnt switch and a zinc question.

PTD-DBM joins a cell-penetrating peptide to a short decoy sequence that stops the protein CXXC5 from binding Dishevelled. Freed from that brake, Wnt/β-catenin signalling rises, and in mice hair regrew faster. Its developers also found CXXC5 raised in human balding scalp. Zinc thymulin is a thymic peptide that is active only when bound to zinc. How it might act on hair has never been defined, and whether any effect would come from the peptide or the zinc is unknown.
PTD-DBM: releases a Wnt brake (mouse data)
Zinc thymulin: a zinc-dependent thymic peptide
Both: mechanism first, human data absent
PTD-DBM
A cell-penetrating tag carries a decoy sequence into follicle cells. The decoy keeps CXXC5 off Dishevelled, so Wnt signalling can rise.
What was shown
Faster hair regrowth, and new follicles in healed wounds, in mice. The work came from the developer's own group, which also found CXXC5 raised in human balding scalp tissue.
Zinc thymulin
A thymic hormone that works only with zinc bound. Its proposed hair effect has no defined mechanism and no indexed human study.

Two peptides are sold for hair, and both arrive with better stories than data. PTD-DBM joins a cell-penetrating fragment borrowed from an HIV protein to a short decoy sequence. Inside follicle cells, the decoy keeps a protein called CXXC5 from binding its partner, Dishevelled, and that releases a brake on Wnt signalling, a pathway involved in hair regrowth. In mice, hair regrew faster and follicles formed in healed wounds. The work came from the developer's own group. Zinc thymulin is a thymic hormone that becomes active only when zinc binds to it. How it might help hair has never been defined, and nobody has shown whether any effect would come from the peptide or from the zinc. Hold both as mechanism, and look for the human trial.
Inside a cell, a small decoy peptide keeps a brake protein from docking on a signalling protein, and small signal tokens move into the nucleus.
The evidence
Zero trials in people.

As of September 2026, PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov list no human trial of PTD-DBM, published or registered. Its evidence is one 2017 study in mice and human scalp tissue from the developer's group, whose senior author is affiliated with a biotech company. A 2025 review's summary speaks of 'clinical efficacy', yet the review's own text describes PTD-DBM results in mouse models only.
human trials of PTD-DBM, published or registered (September 2026)
Lee et al., J Invest Dermatol 2017: mice, plus CXXC5 measured in human scalp tissue
Whether PTD-DBM regrows human hair is unknown. The Peptide Pocket Guide and this course grade it D.

It does not show that PTD-DBM fails or harms. One open safety question sits alongside: the 2025 review flags that off-target Wnt activation is associated with colorectal and liver cancers, a theoretical concern nobody has tested for this peptide.

Module 06 · Opening film
The growth-hormone axis and the skin

Growth hormone and IGF-1 genuinely shape skin, and one peptide on this axis has approval-grade trials. Most of what patients are offered has much less behind it. In three lessons you will separate the physiology from the promise, the approved from the anecdotal, and the side-effects you can see from the risks nobody has measured. Two layers of skin listen to two different parts of the same axis. Growth hormone speaks mainly to the dermis. Its receptor is expressed more on fibroblasts than on keratinocytes, and in culture growth hormone increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis, sometimes directly and sometimes through IGF-1. The epidermis listens to IGF-1. Keratinocytes carry the IGF-1 receptor, their neighbours in the dermis supply the hormone, and in culture IGF-1 makes keratinocytes divide where growth hormone on its own does nothing. With age, growth-hormone pulses and IGF-1 fall steadily, a change called the somatopause. Hold all of this as mechanism. It explains why the axis could matter for skin. Whether changing it helps a patient is a separate question, and the trials answer it.
Lesson 6.1 · Mechanism
Two hormones, two layers of skin.

Growth hormone acts mostly in the dermis. Its receptor is expressed more by fibroblasts than by keratinocytes, and it increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, reaches keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor and makes them divide. Human hair follicles even run their own small growth-hormone loop in the laboratory. With age, GH secretion and IGF-1 fall steadily; this is the somatopause.
GH: dermal fibroblasts and collagen
IGF-1: keratinocyte proliferation, supplied locally
Somatopause: GH and IGF-1 fall with age
The dermis listens to GH
Growth-hormone receptors sit mainly on dermal fibroblasts. GH, directly or through IGF-1, supports fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis.
The epidermis listens to IGF-1
Keratinocytes carry the IGF-1 receptor but make little IGF-1 themselves; fibroblasts supply it. In culture, IGF-1 makes keratinocytes divide and GH on its own does not.
The axis ages
GH pulses and IGF-1 fall from early adulthood. Reference ranges are age-adjusted, so an IGF-1 that is low for a 25-year-old is often normal for the patient's age.

Human evidence
A much-cited skin result, read again.

In 1990 a much-cited New England Journal of Medicine study gave growth hormone for six months to 12 healthy men over 60, with nine untreated men for comparison and no placebo. Lean mass rose and fat fell. Skin thickness rose 7.1%, with P = 0.07, short of statistical significance. A small 1996 randomized trial in 28 older men found 15% more collagen laid down in implanted wound tubes on GH, a laboratory surrogate for repair.
rise in skin thickness in 12 older men given growth hormone for six months (1990)
P = 0.07 · nine untreated men as comparison · no placebo
A skin result still quoted for growth hormone comes from 12 treated men, without a placebo, and it missed statistical significance. Graded on its design, it is D.
It does not show that GH thins skin or that it fails in true deficiency, and it says nothing about secretagogues. It shows how thin the direct skin evidence for growth hormone in healthy ageing is.

Mechanism (D). Cell-culture work from 1992 explains a pathway; it tells you nothing about a patient's skin.
Adults with untreated GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis on biopsy
Human evidence (C), small and observational: 45 people biopsied in 2001. Treatment of childhood-onset deficiency did not fully normalise the skin.
GH shortened donor-site healing in adults with major burns
Human evidence (C): 13 small randomized trials pooled by Cochrane in 2014, with more hyperglycaemia on GH and a risk of bias. Burns over 40% of the body, far from cosmetic use.
Hair follicles keep a GH–IGF-1 loop running outside the body
Mechanism (D). An ex vivo finding from 2023 about follicle biology.
In acromegaly, glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema thicken the skin
Human evidence from disease. It shows what too much growth hormone does to skin, and says nothing about a cosmetic benefit.
Whether raising GH or IGF-1 makes a healthy adult's facial skin look younger
Open question. No randomized trial has measured it, and the 1990 skin result missed statistical significance.
Six sorted. Two are mechanism, three are human evidence, and the one patients ask about is still an open question.
What changes in practice
Deficiency is a diagnosis. Decline is ageing.

In healthy older adults, randomized trials of growth hormone show small shifts in body composition, about 2 kg less fat and 2 kg more lean mass, with more oedema, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and a trend towards diabetes. Strength and endurance change little. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades its advice against treatment A; graded on the trials themselves the evidence is B, and the conclusion is the same. In the US, as of September 2026, knowingly distributing growth hormone for anti-ageing is a federal offence.
Healthy ageing: small body-composition change, more side-effects
Grade B on the trials (guide: A), same conclusion
US: anti-ageing distribution is a federal offence
What the trials show
Pooled randomized trials in healthy older adults: about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass, weight unchanged.
What they cost
More soft-tissue oedema, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia, and a trend towards diabetes. In one trial, 39% of women on GH developed oedema, against none on placebo.
Where it stands
Growth hormone is for diagnosed deficiency and a short list of approved conditions. In the US, distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence.

Here the physiology meets the waiting room. A patient in their fifties has read that growth hormone falls with age and asks whether topping it up would help their skin. The trials in healthy older adults answer that. Pooled, they show about two kilograms less fat and two kilograms more lean mass, with more swelling, joint pain, carpal tunnel symptoms and a drift towards diabetes, while strength and stamina change little. Graded on those trials the evidence is B, consistent and independent though small, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide gives its advice against treatment an A. Both land in the same place. Growth hormone treats a diagnosed deficiency and a short list of approved conditions. In the United States, distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence. Whatever your role, name the decline for what it is, a normal part of ageing.

Prescribe growth hormone only for a confirmed deficiency or another approved indication, usually with an endocrinologist. For a request framed as anti-ageing, document the conversation, the evidence you quoted and the legal position, and decline.
If a patient mentions growth hormone or 'HGH' for skin or energy, record what they use, where it comes from and any swelling, joint pain or tingling, and bring it to the prescriber.

You can explain that growth hormone falls normally with age and that trials in healthy adults show more side-effects than benefit. Anyone who wants to start it needs a prescriber's assessment rather than a product recommendation.
In the UK, somatropin is a prescription-only medicine licensed for growth hormone deficiency and specific growth disorders, and a Class C controlled drug.

In the EU, somatropin medicines have been authorised since the 1980s, through central and national procedures, for growth hormone replacement and for short stature in specific childhood conditions (EMA, 2012). The centrally authorised Omnitrope (since 12 April 2006) is prescription-only, and treatment is started and monitored by a doctor experienced in growth disorders.

In Portugal, somatropin medicines are authorised as restricted-prescription medicines, reserved for conditions diagnosed only in hospital or specialised settings, and INFARMED's register gives them no narcotic classification (25 September 2026). Growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services, and a national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for its administration.

In Brazil, somatropin is registered for replacement therapy in adults with marked growth hormone deficiency, and it is a controlled substance on List C5 (anabolic substances) that needs a special-control prescription in two copies (RDC 1.036/2026). The Federal Council of Medicine's Resolution 1.999/2012, in force in September 2026, bars the use of hormones, including growth hormone, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit.

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has held medicines registration since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023; the medicines law is Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, which prohibits advertising semi-controlled products to the public. Somatropin is registered with the EDE and is on the federal list of semi-controlled medical products (MOHAP Ministerial Decision 306/2023), and every somatropin entry in the EDE register is dispensed as a semi-controlled drug (25 September 2026).

Lesson 6.2 · Concept
One axis, four ways in.

Somatropin is growth hormone itself. GHRH analogues (sermorelin, tesamorelin, CJC-1295) stimulate the pituitary's GHRH receptor. Ghrelin-receptor agonists (ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and the oral ibutamoren, MK-677) stimulate GH release through a second pituitary receptor. IGF-1 analogues such as IGF-1 LR3 bypass the pituitary altogether. They are sold as one family, and the next moments take them apart.
Replace: somatropin
Stimulate: GHRH analogues and ghrelin-receptor agonists
Bypass: IGF-1 analogues
Replace
Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone. It replaces the hormone itself.
Stimulate
GHRH analogues and ghrelin-receptor agonists push the patient's own pituitary to release growth hormone, in pulses.
Bypass
IGF-1 analogues act directly on the IGF-1 receptor, downstream of the pituitary.

Four routes lead into the same axis, and patients rarely know which one they are on. Somatropin is growth hormone itself, made by recombinant technology. GHRH analogues, sermorelin, tesamorelin and CJC-1295, press on the pituitary's releasing-hormone receptor, so the gland releases its own growth hormone in pulses. Ghrelin-receptor agonists, ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and the oral compound ibutamoren, press on a second pituitary receptor. IGF-1 analogues such as IGF-1 LR3 skip the pituitary and act on the IGF-1 receptor directly. Every route ends at that same receptor, which is why lesson three treats their risks together. Clinics often sell all of these as one family with one promise. Keep them apart, because the trials, the approvals and the side-effects belong to each molecule separately.
A hormone axis from the brain to the pituitary, liver and tissue, with four violet entry points: two on the pituitary, one in the bloodstream and one at the tissue itself.

The evidence
Zero skin trials.

A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3. The nearest is a 1997 study of a GHRH(1-29) analogue related to sermorelin, in 19 older adults. Skin thickness measured by caliper rose after 16 weeks, compared with a placebo lead-in rather than a parallel control group.

Lesson 6.3 · Recognition
What too much growth hormone looks like.

Sustained GH excess changes skin in ways you can see. In acromegaly, glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema make the face, hands and feet puffy and thick; the skin turns oily with large pores; sweating increases; skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear. Drugs on this axis bring their own signs: fluid retention with swelling, joint pain, tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. The Endocrine Society recommends measuring IGF-1 when typical acral and facial features are present.
Soft tissue: puffy, thickened face, hands and feet
Skin: oily, sweaty, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans
On treatment: swelling, joint pain, tingling
In the skin
Glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema thicken the skin of the face, hands and feet. Skin turns oily, pores enlarge, sweating increases, and skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear.
In the soft tissues
Hands and feet enlarge slowly and the jaw widens. On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention brings swelling, joint pain and night-time tingling.
When to test

The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 for typical acral and facial features, and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster, including sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis and hypertension.

Excess growth hormone leaves visible marks on skin and soft tissue, and noticing them early matters. In acromegaly, glycosaminoglycan deposits and oedema thicken the face, hands and feet, so features look puffy and coarse. The skin turns oily with large pores, sweating increases, and skin tags and acanthosis nigricans appear. Hands and feet enlarge slowly, and the jaw widens. Drugs on this axis bring their own signs, usually transient, with swelling, joint pain, tingling fingers and carpal tunnel symptoms. On somatropin, the label asks for existing moles to be watched for growth or malignant change. The Endocrine Society recommends measuring IGF-1 when typical acral and facial features are present, and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster. For most of you the job is recognition and referral, and the diagnosis belongs to endocrinology.

Four registers
Does raising IGF-1 cause cancer?
The honest answer has four parts, and each has its own source. Keep them apart, or a mechanism will be heard as a measured risk.
Mechanism
Plausible
IGF-1 receptor signalling drives cell proliferation and survival, which gives any IGF-1-raising product a theoretical concern
Human observation
Modest associations

In large studies, higher natural IGF-1 goes with slightly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer; reverse causation is not excluded. In one Ecuadorian cohort, people with GH-receptor deficiency had almost no cancer.
Acromegaly
Slightly raised, inconsistently
Pooled studies show about 1.5 times the expected cancer incidence, with the highest estimates from small single-centre series; a Danish nationwide cohort found no clear rise
GH replacement
Largely reassuring
No clear raised risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other disease; a 2022 consensus found no link with primary tumours or recurrence in survivors
Open question
Unmeasured
No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin
A plausible mechanism plus a modest association is a reason for caution and consent. It is a different thing from a measured risk.
The evidence
Half the patients on the approved one.

Tesamorelin is the best-studied peptide on this axis. In its pivotal trials, 47% of treated patients had IGF-1 more than two standard deviations above the mean at 26 weeks, and 36% more than three. Its label states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown. For unapproved secretagogues bought for skin, nobody has published the equivalent figure.

A clinic page, read line by line.
Separate the physiology from the promise.
Physiology or promise?
A fictional clinic page for a growth-hormone peptide. Find the lines the evidence does not support.
Growth hormone and IGF-1 fall steadily from early adulthood.
Sound. GH pulses and IGF-1 fall from early adulthood: the somatopause, a normal part of ageing.
If your IGF-1 is below the range for a 30-year-old, your body needs topping up.
Reference ranges are age-adjusted, so an IGF-1 that is low for a 25-year-old is often normal for the patient's age. Treat a diagnosis, not a number read against the wrong age band.
In laboratory studies, growth hormone acts on dermal fibroblasts and supports collagen synthesis.
Sound, as mechanism: in culture growth hormone increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. It explains why the axis could matter for skin, not whether changing it helps a patient.
Our CJC-1295 and ipamorelin injections are clinically proven to thicken skin.
A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3.
Tesamorelin, a peptide on the same axis, is FDA-approved.
Sound, for one use: FDA-approved since 2010 to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
Our blend works the same way, so it carries the same clinical backing.
A GRADE A travels with its indication; the molecule does not carry it anywhere else. Different molecules, different evidence, different regulatory standing.
It is natural and free of side-effects, because it only releases your own growth hormone.

Drugs on this axis bring their own signs: fluid retention with swelling, joint pain, tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. Even tesamorelin, used as labelled in its pivotal trials, pushed IGF-1 more than two standard deviations above the mean in 47% of treated patients.
Look for a true fact stretched into a promise: ageing read as deficiency, mechanism as proof, one molecule's approval as another's, 'your own hormone' as 'safe'.
Three lines are real endocrinology; the other four borrow it for a promise.
